#2822. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2819. Takeaways from Bills win over Vikings

The Buffalo Bills beat the Vikings 23-6 in Week 9 on Monday Night Football, a dominant defensive effort that paired wonderfully with fine performances from Josh Allen and James Cook.

The win moved Joe Brady's team to 7-1 on the season.

These are my takeaways from Buffalo's victory.

The Bills defense had an epic performance in this game, I don't care who the quarterback was. Carson Wentz was 8-of-25 for 81 yards with two picks. And the goalposts can't be moved here. While rumors have swirled of Minnesota trading for a quarterback this past week, there were many who believed the Vikings weren't really downgrading at the position going from Kyler Murray to Wentz for this primetime battle.

Let's not forget, in Week 1, in a relief appearance after Kyler Murray was injured, Wentz was 12-of-19 for 133 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions. On paper, as a veteran pocket passer, he should be better suited for Kevin O'Connell's offense.

And it's not as if Wentz had a pedestrian outing. He had a quarterback rating of 8.9 against the Bills defense. That's the lowest rating a quarterback with at least 25 attempts in a game has managed since… 2019.

Now, of course, Wentz missed on a handful of throws in this contest, but the Bills defense forced him to hold onto the football often — his 2.82-second average time to throw was higher than Josh Allen in this game — with outstanding coverage downfield for the vast majority of this matchup.

The pass rush and coverage were married throughout, and Buffalo only had to blitz on 25.9% of Wentz's dropbacks to affect the pocket consistently.

And I'll finish with this storyline that probably won't be talked about enough given how abysmal the Vikings pass game was — Minnesota ran it 12 times for 51 yards, which equates to a 4.3 yards-per-tote average. Aaron Jones averaged 3.2 yards per carry. Only 27.3% of the Vikings runs were successful — determined by yards gained relative to down and distance — the fifth-lowest rate for a run game in Week 9.

Buffalo's run defense is steadily improving each week, and it's already much more consistent than it was a season ago.

The stats will miss the sheer brilliance of Allen in this game. His rating was only 87.3. But beyond his slightly floated interception — that did come on a 3rd and 23, mind you — the Bills quarterback excelled against the most unique and aggressive defense in football, a truly elite unit, on its home turf.

To start 3-of-5 for 24 yards with a pick and finish the evening 21-of-31 for 234 with a touchdown through the air was immaculate from Allen.

He commanded the offense, both pre and post snap exactly how it should be done. He made smart decisions and threw with proper velocity/touch starting with that touchdown drive near the end of the first half. His ball placement was superb as well.

And, heck, no quarterback is going to be perfect for 60 minutes against that Vikings defense.

Allen did all this without Dion Dawkins and Alec Anderson.

MVP-caliber performance from him in this game.

Grable and Corbett allowed four pressures each. Not exactly what clubs want from starting blockers. But after a few miscommunications early that led to quick pressures, I thought both depth players settled in nicely, and really got after it in the run game in the second half.

The Brian Flores defensive scheme is designed to create offensive line miscommunication, and Grable and Corbett have never played alongside each other in an NFL game before.

But instead of their presence on the field becoming a story throughout this game, an issue that severely hampered the Bills offense all night, Grable and Corbett were steady in the second half, as run and pass blockers.

The responsibilities in Jim Leonhard's defense are starting to become second nature to Terrel Bernard, Dorian Williams, and Kaleb Elarms-Orr.

Williams and Bernard snagged a pick each in this one, and Bernard dropped probably the most gift-wrapped interception opportunity of his NFL career.

They are flowing freely in coverage, rapidly reacting to route concepts, and getting to proper depth at the intermediate level. Against the run, they're triggering quickly and regularly not allowing blocks to stick to them.

In this game, Bernard led the team with six tackles. Dorian Williams had three without a miss. And Elarms-Orr added three tackles of his own on just 13 snaps. This trio has become an underrated three-down group.

Sure, it wasn't idyllic to start. But once Brady understood the outside pitch plays weren't working on the ground, he went away from them.

Then, later, when he realized the interior run game was doing just enough to keep the Vikings defense on its heels and burn clock, he stuck with it.

But it wasn't a one-dimensional attack for Buffalo in this game. There was a fine collection of play-action, throws to tight ends in the flat, running backs involved through the air. Lots of 13 personnel. Over-the-middle looks for Khalil Shakir, some classic first-read looks outside for DJ Moore, and well-timed quick screens to receivers.

Again, it's never going to be flawless against a Flores defense that has the horses on the Vikings roster.

But Brady was in his bag as a play-caller in this convincing win.

Whether it was Tyler Bass making his 18th consecutive field goal (a team record) to begin the season, Tommy Doman Jr. handling punt and kickoff duties and laying the lumber to force a fumble, or Greg Dortch's big return to begin the game, special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers has built a fantastic unit that was showcased in this Monday Night Football win.

In a low-scoring, defensive clash like we got in the first half, I can't stress enough how important Bass making those kicks was to avoid field-position and momentum shifts.

Doman even proved capable of kicking a "dirty ball" that hits within the landing zone but isn't immediately fielded by the returner.

Buffalo's special teams were once again stellar in victory.

#2816. Observations after well-balanced Sixers hold off Bulls

Observations after well-balanced Sixers hold off Bulls originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Still no losing streaks to speak of for the 2026-27 Sixers.

The Sixers earned a 127-121 win Sunday over the Bulls to wrap up a 2-1 road trip. They moved to 9-2 overall and Chicago fell to 1-8.

Every Sixers starter scored in double figures.

Three reached the 20-point mark in Jaylen Brown (29 points), Tyrese Maxey (27 points) and LeBron James (22). Joel Embiid had 18 points and 10 rebounds.

Josh Giddey posted 19 points, 15 assists and seven rebounds for the Bulls.

The Sixers were without Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear). The Bulls' absences included Norman Powell (right shoulder inflammation/soreness) and Zach Collins (respiratory illness).

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a home game Tuesday night vs. the Celtics. Here are observations on their win over Chicago:

Following his 0-for-9 night Friday in the Sixers' loss to the Cavaliers, Embiid did not snap right back into form.

He was well short on his first shot attempt, a wide-open three-pointer. Embiid then failed to score in the post over Jalen Smith.

Embiid got a field goal to go at the 6:42 mark of the first quarter when he tipped in his own miss. However, Smith canned a three on the ensuing possession to give Chicago a 23-16 lead.

James committed two early turnovers, although he did sink a corner three-pointer during a fast-paced first quarter. VJ Edgecombe added two long-range jumpers in the first.

Entering Sunday, the Sixers' minus-9.6 net rating in the first quarter ranked 27th in the NBA. They managed to hold a one-point lead in Chicago after the first.

The Sixers' offensive rebounding was their greatest strength in the first quarter. They poured in 17 second-chance points. Embiid had four offensive boards in the opening frame.

Jabari Walker assumed backup center duties for the second straight game without Bona. He picked up where Embiid left off on the glass, grabbing seven rebounds (three offensive) in a great first stint.

Though he's undersized in the height department for an NBA center at 6-foot-7, Walker has plenty of rebounding tools.

He's listed at a strong 237 pounds, doesn't mind contact whatsoever, hunts the ball, and has a knack for winning contested boards. Walker showed all of that Sunday. Very hard to overstate how well he rebounded.

The Sixers' first-shot offense also had many bright moments in the second quarter.

James got rolling on his way to a 16-point first half, Embiid made a couple of mid-range jumpers, and Maxey hit two free throws put the Sixers up 60-50 late in the second period.

Chicago evened the game at 68-all early in the third quarter on a Matas Buzelis three, but the Bulls couldn't sustain that run.

The Bulls' defense continued to look like one of the worst in the NBA and the Sixers' well-balanced offense kept the scoreboard moving. Brown nailed a turnaround jumper to give his team a double-digit lead. Walker knocked down a top-of-the-key triple to extend the Sixers' advantage to 12 points.

The Sixers had two apparent injury scares in the second half. Brown limped to the sideline with 6:55 to go in the third quarter, but he stayed in the game. Edgecombe headed to the locker room after subbing out at the 9:08 mark of the fourth quarter. He returned to the Sixers' bench and ultimately returned for a final stint.

On the floor, the Sixers couldn't ease to victory. Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson trimmed Chicago's deficit to 116-113 by draining a three. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse called timeout.

The Sixers were efficient enough in the half court down the stretch.

Embiid made a put-back hoop and a pair of free throws. Maxey drilled a side-step three-ball after a wraparound feed from James. The Sixers converted their clutch free throws and secured a winning road trip.

#2813. The Vikings need to trade for a quarterback tomorrow

The biggest test of the still-new partnership between Vikings G.M. Nolan Teasley and Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell has arrived.

What will they do about a team with a Super Bowl-caliber defense and an offense that could barely function in the MAC?

The window remains open until 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday. The Vikings were in this spot three years ago, when Kirk Cousins tore an Achilles tendon two days before the deadline.

That time, the Vikings didn’t have many options; they ended up with Josh Dobbs. This time, there are two former Vikings on other teams who know the Minnesota offense: Colts quarterback Daniel Jones and Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins.

If the calls haven’t already been made, they should be. Immediately. What will it take to salvage a season that is disintegrating before everyone’s eyes, despite the 6-2 record?

It wouldn’t be easy to plug and play a new quarterback, but there’s history with Jones and Cousins. It would be easier to get them up to speed than if they brought in someone who would be learning everything from scratch.

If, in the end, the Colts want too much for Jones and the Raiders want too much for Cousins (neither is untouchable; the question is the amount of the compensation), the only other starter potentially available would be Geno Smith.

Some have suggested a play for Justin Herbert. At this point, however, it’s impossible to know whether his implosion is about his surroundings or about Herbert.

Then there’s Jimmy Garoppolo, who remains a free agent — and who has been largely forgotten.

Whatever the Vikings do, staying the course with Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz is a middle finger to the fan base. And Max Brosmer, by all appearances, isn’t good enough to make a difference.

The fans know it. The boos were frequent, loud, and warranted on Monday night.

And, perhaps more importantly, when will the narrative change about O’Connell being a quarterback whisperer? He didn’t want 2024 first-rounder J.J. McCarthy, who had fallen to third on the depth chart before he was given away for a fifth-round draft pick. O’Connell preferred Murray, who has been underwhelming. Wentz landed at No. 2 on the depth chart, and when the lights got bright Wentz winced..

It’s a pivotal moment for Teasley, O’Connell, and the entire franchise. They can continue to act like everything is fine, that 6-2 is a good record, whatever.

Anyone who’s paying attention knows the truth. The Vikings, after starting 6-0, are sinking like a smooth stone in a septic tank. Failure to act amounts to dysfunction.

And, yes, dysfunctional teams do dysfunctional things. Some around the league have suggested in recent years that the Vikings are low-key dysfunctional.

Right or wrong, they’re definitely the worst 6-2 team we’ve ever seen — and the only question at this point is whether they’ll figure out how to win another game.

#2812. Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup

Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers couldn't rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers.

They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4.

The Sixers' top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17).

The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley.

The Sixers' injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury.

With Friday's loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat.

The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland:

After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam.

The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers' Oct. 22 win over Cleveland, they were many levels below their best in the first quarter.

The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers' chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid's larger problem was that he couldn't hit any sort of shot besides free throws.

He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds.

Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he's now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that's bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season.

Of course, it's notable that Embiid's been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We'll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out.

James didn't play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers.

As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc.

Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers' rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures.

With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland's lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass.

Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals.

Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers' comeback push.

The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk.

With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons, Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game.

Still, the Sixers' offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points.

Embiid didn't play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He's had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career, back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors.

Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they'd hit speed bumps throughout the year. They'll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

#2811. Green Bay Packers News: Packers prep for NFL trade deadline

Welcome to NFL Trade Deadline day! All trades need to be finalized by 4 p.m. Eastern time today as teams try to make the last-minute moves they think they need to become contenders or stockpile future assets.

We've already seen quite a few moves leading up to the deadline with a few big-name players arriving at new teams, but the eternal question in these parts is whether or not the Packers will do anything.

Certainly the Packers have needs. They could use some help on the offensive line, even as the guard situation seems to stabilize, and a running back with any amount of actual juice would be a blessing. And, if you believe the rumors going around, they've been sniffing around just about any trade-worth defensive lineman with a pulse.

But the question is whether or not any of those moves would actually fix anything for them. Would throwing a new running back behind the offensive line as it's presently constituted actually improve the running game? That seems doubtful, and I'm skeptical of the idea that they could add any linemen who would make a real difference, either. And there's also the question of price. Take Jonathan Taylor, for instance. He'd definitely be a better running back option than anything the Packers currently have, but it sounds like it's going to take a king's ransom to pry him out of Indianapolis.

The best intersection of price and value might be on the defensive line, but even then price is a huge consideration, since the Packers are already without a first round pick next year. Brian Gutekunst has gone on record about his high opinion of the 2027 draft class, and that seems to be the consensus view. Would he really surrender another valuable pick for a short-term player?

The Packers, again, undeniably have needs. But what it'd take to fix them might take them out of the trade market this year.

Teams looking for a receiver should make the call.

#2803. Rams' dream season has been a survival test. Now Puka Nacua is out | Opinion

If the NFL playoffs were today, guess who would be at home watching?

The Los Angeles Rams. The offseason champs. The team bookies installed as the betting favorite to play Super Bowl 61 in their own stadium – before L.A. was thrashed by the 49ers in their season opener in Australia, before all sorts of other stuff since then hit the fan.

So far, this season of destiny for the Rams – who climbed above .500 (5-4) for the first time this season on Sunday – has become an exercise in Murphy's Law.

And more bad news came on Monday when the team confirmed that star wideout Puka Nacua is headed to injured reserve after suffering sprained ligaments in his right knee and a turf toe. He will miss at least a month.

It figures that Nacua was injured running a jet sweep on, of all times, the final offensive play of the 20-13 victory at Washington.

"I'm bummed," Rams coach Sean McVay told reporters at the team's headquarters on Monday. "When these things happen, the first thing is you feel for the players. They put so much work in and it's so unfortunate.

"Then you question, 'What could you have done to maybe avoid it?' "

The Rams just can't win for losing one way or another. After all, Nacua's star receiving mate, Davante Adams, is already on IR, mending a ruptured hamstring. Cornerback Trent McDuffie, one of the prized offseason additions, has missed the past three games due to a back issue layered on top of a groin injury. Jaylen Watson, the other prized cornerback from the offseason haul, is done for the year because of shoulder surgery. The O-line just lost left guard Steve Avila to a hamstring injury with no definitive timeline for a return. And Myles Garrett, the reigning Defensive Player of the Year obtained from the Browns in a blockbuster trade, just came back on Sunday after missing two months following knee surgery.

The midseason checkup on McVay's team is brutal. They have become the Bad News Rams, complete with inexplicable losses. They blew a 16-0 halftime lead at Denver in Week 3, punctuated by Matthew Stafford's record-setting pick-six. They lost against Buffalo in Week 5 after since-released kicker Harrison Mevis' 48-yard try for a game-winning field in overtime was blocked. Six days later, the defense didn't give up a touchdown. But the Rams lost to Arizona, anyway, when Chad Ryland kicked his sixth field goal of the game as time expired.

They could've, would've and should've won all three of those games. All losses.

You can't blame Aaron Donald, the Hall of Fame-credentialed D-tackle who came out of retirement after a two-year layoff, if he wondered: I came back for this?

For all the adversity, though, it would be foolish to write off the Rams just yet.

Over the past three seasons, eight teams have made the playoffs after being .500 or worse through their first eight games. The Rams were two of those teams, rallying from a 3-5 start in 2023 and a 4-4 mark in 2024. And L.A., during the 2021 season, was also the last team to earn a Super Bowl berth without being one of the top three seeds in its conference.

Then again, limping into the playoffs is no formula for a Super Bowl ticket.

One thing for certain: the fiery McVay (whose late grandfather, John, was the personnel whiz attached to Bill Walsh as they launched the 49ers dynasty during the 1980s) will have his competitive creativity gene stretched to the hilt while trying to build on a three-game winning streak.

Nacua caught 14 passes on 19 targets for 150 yards on Sunday to raise his season totals to 70 receptions for 715 yards. And now, without Adams, the Rams must replace that production?

"We won't have some tendencies, that's for sure," McVay said. "We'll figure out what that looks like to be able to get the best different groupings and best people involved. Guys will be asked to step up."

That's the NFL way. It's a war of attrition. Although the Rams' issues are undoubtedly pronounced, every team has some level of injury-related challenges. At one extreme, the Ravens are collapsing without star quarterback Lamar Jackson. The Giants, meanwhile, are hanging tough after absorbing the "shock sandwich," as John Harbaugh described it, of losing quarterback Jaxson Dart and linebacker Brian Burns, the team's best defensive player. At the other end of the spectrum, the 49ers have a share of the NFL's best record (7-1) while battling through setbacks that include the extended absence of defensive end Nick Bosa and the decimation of a receiving corps that includes Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel.

So, no, the Rams get no pity from their bitter NFC West rival.

They also have much company in the misery department when it comes to teams pegged as contenders when this season began. The defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks (5-4) wouldn't be in the playoffs right now, either, challenged to find a way on offense to complement the greatness of Jaxon Smith-Njigba. The defending AFC champion Patriots (5-4) are three games in the loss column behind the Bills in the AFC East race. The Cowboys? It's apparent the Super Bowl drought will continue, going on 31 years. And the NFC East drought rolls on, too.

And no, there were no quick fixes from the trade market (not for the Rams, unlike the Bears and Jaguars), even with GM Les Snead's typically deft maneuvering with personnel moves. Shoot, even if there were, the premium draft capital to exchange has already been used.

Adjustments and growth from within will determine L.A.'s fate. Perhaps the battle-tested team, stocked with savvy vets, can get key players back from injury and jell at the right time to make a run down the stretch.

It won't be easy. After a bye in Week 11, the Rams face the Packers, Chiefs and 49ers in a three-game test. Two of their final three games are against the Seahawks. Yes, there's a lot of football left to close the gap and make a legit run for the postseason.

Never mind that so much was expected of this team before the season started.

"I think it's about just improving every single day," McVay said. "Every single game it's let's reset, reload, six seconds at a time."

In the meantime, the Super Bowl vision that so many had for the Rams will be measured on a different type of clock during the second half of the season to avoid a 10-count.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Rams' dream season has been a survival test. Now Puka Nacua is out | Opinion

#2794. Did Commanders lose the Rams game when they released starting center Tyler Biadasz in February? - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Prior to the start of the season, not many people would have expected the Commanders to beat a Rams team consisting of Matthew Stafford, Puka Nacua, Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett. But the Rams were 4-4 entering the game and it was a game very much there for the taking. The Commanders defense held up relatively well, but the offense struggled to get much going after a strong start.

One of the biggest issues the Commanders had on offense was the protection plan. The Rams had star pass rusher Myles Garrett back healthy after he missed most of the season injured. It was the first time the Rams had Garrett and star defensive tackle Aaron Donald on the field together. It's a formidable pair. Donald may well go down in NFL history as the best interior defensive lineman ever and Garrett might well become the best edge rusher in NFL history. Both are freak athletes and are incredibly hard for even the best offensive lineman to block one-on-one.

With such a strong pair of defensive lineman, it would make sense to build an entire game plan around preventing those two players from blowing up the entire offense. The last time the Commanders faced Garrett was in 2024, Jayden Daniels' rookie season. Kliff Kingsbury was the offensive coordinator then and he put together a strong game plan to try and negate Garrett's effectiveness. They used run plays, read-option plays, run-pass option plays (RPOs), multiple forms of misdirection, screens. Kingsbury also made sure to play with lots of tempo to tire out Garrett and used no-huddle to attack when Garrett wasn't on the field and stop him from subbing back in.

Most importantly, Kingsbury made sure to get a second pair of hands on him on almost every play. They would slide the line his way when they could, but they would always chip him. Everyone had a go at chipping him, receivers, tight ends and running backs. He never knew exactly who was going to chip him on any given play because of how often they switched it up. It was a terrific plan and Garrett failed to register a single stat in the game, which is a large part of why the Commanders were able to win that game back in 2024.

Now, this game in 2026 is a different animal because the Rams also have Aaron Donald to worry about. But offensive coordinator David Blough was on Kingsbury's staff back in 2024 and I had hoped he might have learned some lessons from Kingsbury's plan to help deal with Garrett. Unfortunately, the protection plan was poor and nothing like that 2024 plan.

The two most basic weapons you have in pass protection are chips and line slides. Chips are where you have a tight end, running back or occasionally a wide receiver align tight to the formation and bump the edge rusher before releasing into their routes. Line slides are when either all of the line, or at least part of it, slides to one side, providing extra help to that side. Far too often in this game, the Commanders didn't use either of these weapons.

Lucas Patrick's concussion sent rookie Matt Gulbin in against Myles Garrett while Nick Allegretti stayed on the sideline

[Washington's] latest issue on the offensive line stems from the center position: this past weekend, when their starter Lucas Patrick went down with a concussion, they turned to rookie Matt Gulbin. It's ironic because Adam Peters and Dan Quinn spent the offseason trying to convince everyone that Nick Allegretti was that guy and would be the center for 2026. Allegretti has played two snaps since his last start, which came at right guard against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 3. In other words, he's still the same journeyman offensive lineman who came here years ago looking for a chance to start, but better suited as a backup. They tried to sell the fanbase a pumpkin, hoping Cinderella logic would kick in and he'd turn into something more than a dried-up gourd that rots on a warm fall night.

When asked about the situation Sunday after the game, Quinn said the staff has been working Allegretti more at guard now: "In that moment, I would have felt comfortable with Nick as well, but I thought, let's give the guy who's got the most reps." Quinn also confirmed Allegretti was healthy. It makes sense that the coach would turn to the player who has practiced the most in the role; the problem is he said this in the preseason: "Nick is one of our smartest players, so that's a position that you rely on." Relied on so much that when the team looks for a replacement weeks later in crunch time with the season on the line, they turn to the sixth-round prospect with very little experience. Gulbin gave up a 12-yard sack to Myles Garrett on third-and-5 at the Rams' 38, leaving Washington facing fourth-and-17, but who could be mad at a rookie who should have been given more help on that play? The Commanders' protection plan failed when it mattered most Sunday.

Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app.

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Look, the Commanders didn't lose to the Rams 20-13 solely because Patrick got dinged up and Gulbin had to replace him, tasked with trying to help block Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald when he hadn't played in more than a month and had essentially just one game of experience in his NFL career.

"It's an excuse," Gulbin said afterward. "I got to go out and do the expectations for the center position. I got to go out there and block them. And I don't think I did a great job."

Credit for self-awareness. The situation is not of Gulbin's making, and he can only perform the job in adverse circumstances to the best of his ability.

But we're focusing on Gulbin's participation and Patrick's injury and Allegretti's absence because — well, in some way, the center position drove the talk around Washington's entire offseason. And here it is, November now, with the Commanders' season on the brink at 2-5-1, and it's still dogging them as they head into a short week with a season's-over-if-you-lose game at the New York Giants on Thursday night.

This all sounds familiar, and some of it is definitely a rehash of old material. But it matters. It matters because, with the Commanders trailing by a touchdown and facing third-and-5 late in the fourth quarter, Garrett — playing for the first time in nearly two months — came from his position on the edge to rush up the middle.

The issue isn't that a rookie taken in the sixth round came in as an emergency replacement and couldn't block Myles Garrett. The issue is how we got here. This will be playin' the hits, to a certain extent. But it's worth going over for the umpteenth time.

The pared-down version: The Commanders cut Tyler Biadasz. They pursued Tyler Linderbaum. They lost out to the Las Vegas Raiders — understandably — because who wants to spend $81 million on a center?

Then they leaned in — hard — on the idea Allegretti could be their center. The week before the Commanders opened their season in Philadelphia, general manager Adam Peters sat for a Q&A session with radio hosts Grant Paulsen and Danny Rouhier of 106.7 The Fan in front of a live audience. They joked about how much of the offseason had been spent discussing the center position, particularly after Allegretti missed most of training camp with a calf strain.

Allegretti started in the opener at the Philadelphia Eagles. Two days later, the Commanders signed Patrick — cut Aug. 30 by the Giants — as a free agent. In Week 3, Patrick started at guard, alongside Allegretti at center. By the Week 4 game in London, Patrick took over at center.

The Commanders have been trying to put together a complete game all season. Nine weeks later, they are still searching for such a game.

Washington got out to a good enough start in the first half. It was not perfect — they still had pre-snap penalties and a turnover — but it was enough to outperform a talented Rams team that was sluggish to start the afternoon. Jayden Daniels was 6-of-7 during the offense's first two drives and threw a seven-yard touchdown to Van Jefferson.

The Rams found little success outside of the field goal on their opening drive with back-to-back three-and-outs in the second quarter. The Rams ended the half with another field goal, but it remained a four-point lead in Washington's favor.

The second half, however, was a different story. The Rams didn't do much more, but the two touchdowns they scored at the top of the third and fourth quarters were enough to give them a lead that Washington could not overcome. The Commanders' offense did little in the third quarter with just 20 yards on 10 plays. There was more production in the final 15 minutes, but the results were much the same: a punt, a turnover on downs and a fumble.

Washington finished the day with 313 yards, 157 of which came on three of their 11 possessions. The Rams were only marginally better, but they generated six more first downs and converted all three of their fourth-down attempts. As head coach Dan Quinn alluded after the game, the Commanders must keep searching for an answer until they find one.

There was an eminently winnable game at Northwest Stadium Sunday, against a good but hardly great Los Angeles Rams team, and a chance to stay, sort of, in the NFC East race. The Commanders scored on their first two possessions, with a lot of game left to add more, especially after the defense took the ball away from Los Angeles twice. Instead, almost 45 minutes of futility, plus Puka Nacua, followed, as did a 20-13 loss. It's not the end of the season, but the end is a short Uber ride from 2-5-1. (Hey, there's still a 6 percent chance. Stop whining.)

"Once again, we have not nailed our complementary football, and I will keep saying that until we do," coach Dan Quinn said. "We're halfway through the season, and that all has to click."

Quinn has said some version of this after just about every game so far this season. Yet, other than center Nick Allegretti (more on him below) and corner Mike Sainristil, almost no one's been replaced in the rotation after subpar play.

From a different article published by The Athletic:

When asked if the persistent mistakes could lead to personnel changes, Quinn indicated it could soon head that way, but that doing so ahead of Thursday night's game would be difficult.

"Yeah, it's a fair question and that's what I'm trying to dig into to find it," he said Monday. "It is a little more challenging on a shorter week than not, but just because the reps are quick. … So, at this time, I'm trying to look at it collectively. What do we need to do to put people in the best spots to do their thing? And if we get past that and find shortcomings in that way, then no, I would not hesitate."

Daniels and the offense were shorthanded Sunday, playing without three of their top receivers. Terry McLaurin's lost for the season, of course, but Washington lost Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown to injuries this week, too. There wasn't a lot of YAC left in the receiver room.

With left tackle Laremy Tunsil out since training camp, Washington turned to third-year lineman Brandon Coleman to replace him. Coleman played well there at times as a rookie in 2024. But he's has struggled badly this season with false starts. He had two more Sunday. The Commanders keep rolling him out there.

The penalties aren't all on Coleman. A new offense has new cadences pre-snap. Sometimes it's hard to hear exactly what the quarterback is saying out there. Washington used its bye week, Quinn said, to try cutting some of those cadences down and make it easier for the O-linemen to communicate with one another. But Sunday, the line was again jumbled.

Remember: The Commanders cut Tyler Biadasz, their starting center last season, last winter. They never really have said why, but it doesn't matter now.

The line struggled, mightily, in the second half against the soon-to-be Hall of Fame duo of Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett, the latter returning to action Sunday after being on injured reserve for most of the season. In the second quarter, Washington's defense turned the game's momentum when K'Lavon Chaisson stripped Nacua after a catch, and safety Nick Cross recovered the fumble with 2:34 left. The Commanders had first-and-10 at the Rams' 40; up 10-3, Washington was set up to increase its lead to two scores just before the half.

The definition of "must-win" changes throughout the season. Some would argue—probably most rightfully—that a "must-win" game is only ever a game where your season is legitimately on the line. I have sliced that deli meat a little finer, instead arguing that through the middle of the season, teams have different possible season outcomes available to them.

For example, for the Commanders to have meaningfully expected to be part of the wild-card chase, that must-win game has almost certainly passed us by (and we lost it). The weak NFC East, however, has kept the Commanders in the playoff picture, offering the more traditional route to a playoff spot as division winners.

With the New York Giants and Dallas Cowboys winning yesterday, I think it's safe to say that Thursday Night Football is a must-win game for the Commanders. A loss to the Giants would give us six losses, with at least a few opponents still on the schedule against whom we will be significant underdogs.

Coaches and players understandably resist labeling games as must-win affairs, especially when elimination isn't technically on the line. But Washington has reached the point where such distinctions are becoming meaningless.

"Yeah, I think next week is a must-win," quarterback Jayden Daniels said following Sunday's 20-13 loss.

"Damn right," edge rusher K'Lavon Chaisson said postgame when asked if there was concern over the season slipping away. "Obviously, you want to stay competitive, stay in that race, to play football throughout the year. We never want to neglect that or seem like that's not the goal. So, it's something that we want to clean up with urgency.

"That's our word throughout the year. We have to clean up the self-inflicted wounds."

Losing to the 5-2-1 Giants at MetLife Stadium would drop the Commanders four games back, effectively more with New York owning the head-to-head tiebreaker.

[A]fter coming up short against the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday and falling to 2-5-1, the Commanders have almost run out of opportunities. Their season, and maybe even the fate of their head coach, will come to a head Thursday night, when they face the New York Giants on the road.

Washington sits three games behind the Giants in the NFC East and has the second-worst record in the conference. Its playoff chances have oscillated between "not great" and "barely there" in recent weeks, allowing the team to cling to some hope while knowing a run would require a small miracle.

A win on Thursday wouldn't be enough to make the playoffs suddenly attainable. But it would at least get the Commanders back to two games out of first place, at 3-5-1 — and owning a head-to-head tiebreaker over the Giants.

[W]hile it's highly unlikely the team will lose their final eight games and finish 2-15 this year, it's difficult right now to envision how they're ever going to win again.

When all is said and done, will this be the worst Eagles team of the last 40 years? There are four other squads they'll have to contend with for that dubious honor. Let's take a look at how this year's Eagles, through nine games, compare with the very worst of the last four decades.

[T]he 1998 season is quite clearly the worst team the franchise has fielded in the last 40 years, and it actually isn't all that close. Ray Rhodes' final campaign was an utter disaster. Their -183 point differential and -11.4 point margin of victory drove their -12.8 SRS that was far and away the lowest of any of the five teams we're discussing.

As painful as the 2026 offense has been to watch, Rhodes' '98 team averaged 10.1 points per game against one of the easiest schedules in the NFL that season. Koy Detmer, Bobby Hoying and Rodney Peete "led" an offense that scored 20+ points just ONCE , in a Week 4 24-21 loss to the Chiefs. They didn't score more than 17 points in any of their final 12 games, and they were shut out three times that season. Somehow Duce Staley ran for 1,065 yards, and Jeff Graham was their top receiver in yards (600). They threw 7 touchdowns as a team and tossed 18 INTs.

So much can happen, both good and bad. But right now, here are my rankings, from worst-to-"first":

[C]ould the move indicate there's potential for Jim Schwartz to return to Philly?

According to Eagles beat reporter Jeff McLane, the team had privately reached out to Jim Schwartz earlier in the year when DC Vic Fangio was contemplating retirement. Moving on from Davis could indicate Fangio is once again considering walking away, and Schwartz's scheme and personnel needs may already be impacting the Eagles' roster-building decisions.

Even former Eagles legend Brandon Graham spoke about the possibility of Schwartz returning to Philly on the PHLY post-game show — right next to BGN's Brandon Lee Gowton —, saying that they have the guys his former DC would be able to maximize.

The Jaguars sent a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Eagles for Davis, who was the No. 13 pick in 2022 — taken 12 spots behind former Georgia teammate and current Jaguars defensive end Travon Walker.

We just mentioned it, but the Ferguson touchdown really was quite fortunate. In that respect it really bailed Brian Schottenheimer out.

That touchdown came on fourth and short in the redzone, but the third down play that Brian Schottenheimer called right before it was so silly. While the Cowboys were gashing the Colts their play-caller decided to call a trick play for CeeDee Lamb that lost yardage. You can argue that the decision to go for it on fourth down, even though it worked out, was pressing a bit.

This doesn't even cover the fact that the Cowboys barely beat a really bad Colts team. Heck, they were losing to the team in question late in the game. They almost did lose. Schottenheimer's squad pulled this one off with zero room to spare. He has to be better.

[Note: The Commanders play the Vikings in Week 16]

Having lost consecutive games after a 6-0 start, will they use the Tuesday afternoon NFL trade deadline to add a quarterback? Or will they try to make it work for the rest of this season with a combination of Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer?

Coach Kevin O'Connell deferred the question to general manager Nolan Teasley after Monday night's 23-6 loss to the Buffalo Bills. It was the third game this season that the Vikings failed to score a touchdown, a level of production that has threatened to waste high-level play from their defense and special teams.

Wentz completed only 8 of 25 passes for 81 yards while throwing two interceptions and having a third dropped. His 2.3 QBR was the lowest for any quarterback this season and the lowest by a Vikings quarterback since Tarvaris Jackson recorded a 1.8 QBR during a game in 2006. It was also the lowest in a "Monday Night Football" game since Sam Darnold posted a 1.1 QBR in 2019 while playing for the New York Jets against the New England Patriots, a game where he was recorded saying he was "seeing ghosts."

"I haven't had many starts over the last couple years in general," Wentz said, "but this one felt pretty terrible. I'm not going to lie. Yeah, this one wasn't my favorite, that's for sure."

Wentz' disaster class wastes Flores' masterclass. Kyler Murray's hamstring injury opened up the possibility that Carson Wentz might step up in prime time and prove himself a more effective quarterback for Minnesota's offense, which had struggled to find much traction under the two-time Pro Bowler. He did the exact opposite of that, ridding Vikings fans of any notion that there was a QB on the bench who represented a better option.

Facing the 30th-ranked defense against the pass, Wentz delivered a miserable performance. He missed pass catchers short, high and wide. He threw one interception deep to T.J. Hockenson where only Bills linebacker Dorian Williams could catch it, and another one directly to LB Terrel Bernard while trying to hit Justin Jefferson. He went 3 of 8 on short throws (0-9 yards air yards) and 3 of 13 on anything deeper than that, finishing 8 of 25 overall for 81 yards and an 8.9 passer rating — the lowest by any QB to attempt at least 25 passes in a game since Sam Darnold's 3.6 passer rating during his 2019 "seeing ghosts" outing, per NFL Research.

Despite all that, Minnesota's tremendous defense kept it to a one-possession game until 6:17 remained. A two-play first-quarter sequence perhaps most accurately represents how brutally Wentz offset his team's defensive efforts. Byron Murphy made a stellar interception, playing center field on a Josh Allen end zone prayer, to kill Buffalo's second drive. He even returned it to midfield to put Wentz and Co. on the doorstep of field goal range. Instead, on the very next snap, Wentz carelessly whipped a wide receiver screen to Jefferson that went both backward and too high. Jefferson couldn't corral it and the Bills recovered the fumble to get the ball right back.

That set the tone for a most disappointing day. The QB position has been a massive problem for the Vikings in 2026. They overcame it in their first six games, but an inept offense has now cost them two straight. They must fix it, either in house or before the trade deadline, before it's too late.

The Rams likely will place wide receiver Puka Nacua on injured reserve with an MCL and PCL sprain in his right leg, as well as turf toe, coach Sean McVay said Monday.

McVay didn't give a specific timeline for how many weeks Nacua is expected to miss, but said the team believes it will be at least a month.

Nacua was hurt on the Rams' final offensive snap of Sunday's victory over the Washington Commanders. The injuries happened on third down with the Rams attempting to end the game with a conversion. Nacua rushed for 5 yards but took a hard hit on the play and briefly stayed on the ground before walking off the field.

Nacua had 14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown in the victory. He was targeted 19 times by quarterback Matthew Stafford. The Rams were already without wide receiver Davante Adams, who suffered a hamstring injury in Week 6.

McVay said Monday he's "kicking himself" in retrospect about exposing Nacua to a big hit with a run play late with a 20-13 lead.

[Note: It took until the final play of regulation for the 'superteam' to secure a 7-point win against the 2-win Commanders on Sunday]

The Rams had their would-be Dream Team on the field Sunday at Northwest Stadium, or at least the closest version to it that they've had all season.

Myles Garrett made his return from knee surgery to join Aaron Donald for the first time on the Rams' defense, giving that unit an imposing duo with a combined five NFL Defensive Player of the Year awards and total estimated career NFL earnings of $368.4 million, according to Spotrac.

On offense, quarterback Matthew Stafford, the NFL's reigning MVP, was throwing passes to standout wide receiver Puka Nacua. This was the way it was supposed to be when the Rams made an offseason trade with the Browns to get Garrett, welcomed back Donald from retirement and entered the season as the unquestioned Super Bowl favorite in a bid to reprise their "Fuck Them Picks" championship run in the 2021 season.

The result Sunday was a 20–13 win over the Commanders that continued the Rams' recent resurgence in an unexpectedly inconsistent season. Garrett had three sacks while playing in his first game since the season opener. Donald was held without a sack in his first game alongside Garrett.

[Note: The Commanders play the Cardinals in Week 12]

The Cardinals' offense took two major blows Monday.

Quarterback Gardner Minshew II probably needs season-ending surgery on his right ulnar collateral ligament, sources told ESPN, and wide receiver Michael Wilson will sit out the rest of the season because of a neck injury, coach Mike LaFleur said.

Sources told ESPN that Minshew is seeking additional medical opinions to confirm whether he'll need the UCL surgery.

Minshew was injured on a hit on the last play of the first half from Seattle Seahawks linebacker Dante Fowler Jr. Fowler hit Minshew as he was throwing, forcing a fumble. Minshew appeared to be in pain on the ground and then as he walked off to the locker room at the intermission but continued to play for the rest of the game.

With Minshew expected to be out, the Cardinals are set to turn to rookie quarterback Carson Beck on Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams. The team also plans to sign veteran Josh Johnson off the Cincinnati Bengals' practice squad, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter.

A source told ESPN that Wilson fractured a vertebra and was expected to be in a brace for the next six weeks to two months. LaFleur said he's not worried about Wilson's injury being long term.

Wilson is the latest Cardinals receiver to be lost.

After trading Marvin Harrison Jr. to the Houston Texans in Week 5, the Cardinals lost Jalen Brooks and Kendrick Bourne for the season because of wrist and ankle injuries, respectively. Arizona is now down to Simi Fehoko, Devin Duvernay, Reggie Virgil and Harrison Wallace III as its only active receivers.

LaFleur said he has never experienced as many injuries at a single position as he has this season.

[Kyle Shanahan continues to answer questions about the receiver like a prissy little bitch]

The NFL reinstated San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk on Monday after he reported for a physical, according to the league's transaction wire.

The wire also states that the Niners have received a two-game roster exemption to sort through any remaining business with Aiyuk. That exemption expires Monday, Nov. 23, after San Francisco's Week 11 game against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City.

"It means absolutely nothing to our team," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "I think we got two-week roster exemption and that's all administrative stuff to me."

San Francisco has three options. It could release Aiyuk, the scenario that has remained the most plausible throughout the offseason. It could trade Aiyuk, which has long been its preferred option, but it hasn't found a trade partner and the deadline for a deal is Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET.

Finally, it could keep Aiyuk and put him on the 53-man roster, though that ship seemed to sail long ago with Shanahan indicating as much Friday afternoon.

Asked what he would like to see happen in the meeting between the team and Aiyuk, Shanahan said he couldn't "care less."

[Note: The Commanders play the Jaguars in Week 17]

The Jaguars have made a splash move to shore up the back end of their defense.

Jacksonville acquired Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates from the Atlanta Falcons in exchange for a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, the team announced Monday.

ESPN's Adam Schefter first reported the news.

The Falcons are paying most of Bates' salary to complete the deal, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport added.

Jacksonville wasn't done raiding the NFC South on Monday, later acquiring defensive tackle Davon Godchaux from the New Orleans Saints, Schefter and NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe reported. Schefter added that the Saints will receive a conditional 2028 sixth-round draft pick in the deal. The selection can turn into a 2027 sixth-rounder if Jacksonville were to acquire one.

The Jacksonville Jaguars are going all-in on a Super Bowl push.

The Jags are trading for Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis, sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round selection to Philadelphia, the teams announced on Monday.

The deal marks the third trade for a defensive player of the day for the Jaguars after acquiring Falcons safety Jessie Bates and Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.

It's a stunning flurry of moves from Jaguars general manager James Gladstone, who surrendered tremendous draft capital (five total picks, including a first and two seconds) to revamp his team's defense a day before the league's trade deadline.

The moves on Monday were made to combat the season-ending injuries to starting safety Eric Murray and defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton with Godchaux and Davis providing a new interior tandem for defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile.

#2793. Patriots CB Christian Gonzalez had a game so bad, he did something never seen before

When Christian Gonzalez signed a four-year, $135 million contract with the Patriots before the season, it was a new record for a cornerback. On Sunday, Gonzalez set a very different kind of record.

According to Next Gen Stats, which uses player tracking to determine which defensive back is in coverage on every pass thrown in every game, Gonzalez had a bad game against two Packers receivers that was unlike anything seen before.

Gonzalez allowed seven catches for 105 yards to Packers wide receiver Matthew Golden, and three catches for 82 yards to Packers wide receiver Christian Watson. Gonzalez is the only defender, as far back as Next Gen Stats go (since at least 2018) to allow more than 80 receiving yards in coverage to two different players in the same game.

Head coach Mike Vrabel said the Patriots expect better from Gonzalez, and he expects better from himself. The Patriots need to be better on Sunday, when they’re playing a Lions offense that also focuses its passing game around two big-play wide receivers, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams. They must be licking their chops watching film of Gonzalez this week.

#2791. Nmecha defends controversial goal celebration after criticism

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha has defended his controversial goal celebration and said he doesn't want to exclude anyone with his religious belief.

"With my celebration, I don't want to put myself or any organization in the foreground. Rather, it's about putting down my "crown" in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength," Nmecha said on Instagram.

"My message was never focused on promoting intolerance, discrimination or hatred in any form."

Nmecha's recurring goal celebration, in which he takes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling, has been criticized by Dortmund's fan department.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. And faith should also not be misused to fail to recognize the diversity of the society in which we live," the Dortmund fan department, an official section of the club's hierarchy, said in a statement on Sunday.

"It is not about condemning a person for their faith. Our criticism is directed at religious networks that spread a worldview under the cloak of faith in which people are devalued or excluded because of their sexual orientation, their gender identity, their way of life or their personal choices."

The club has announced talks with the player and according to broadcasters WDR, citing Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke, Nmecha is to refrain from celebrating the goal in that manner in the future.

Furthermore, BVB intends to contact the Ballers in God group to stop prominently advertising with the player.

Ballers in God is a network of Christian footballers founded in 2015 that records and shares many such celebrations on social media.

Nmecha has previously been criticized for religious content on social media, which has been deemed homophobic. He has rejected these accusations.

#2788. Greg Rousseau: Bills defense showing "what we can do" over last two weeks

The Bills gave up at least 29 points in five of their first six games of the season and opponents averaged over 386 yards of offense in those contests.

Concern about those numbers was mitigated by the team’s 5-1 record, but it lingered as a reason to doubt that the Bills would be able to go the distance come the postseason. The Bills had a bye in Week 7 and the last two weeks have seen very different performances.

The Bills allowed 144 yards in a 36-10 win over the Ravens in Week 8 and they allowed 178 in Monday night’s 23-6 win over the Vikings. They recorded six sacks and six takeaways in those games and the defensive effort on Monday bought their offense time to get going after a poor start to the game.

Linebacker Greg Rousseau had a sack in each win to get to eight for the season and he said the performances show a unit that is discovering its identity.

“Last week wasn’t a fluke,” Rousseau said, via Lance Lysowski of the Buffalo News. “It’s what we are. It’s what we can do. We just have to keep going.”

The counter to Rousseau or anyone else feeling bullish about the Bills defense is that Joe Fagnano was at quarterback for most of the Ravens game and that Carson Wentz was running the Vikings offense. The Bills can’t control such things, of course, but they do make it harder to feel like the results were all about tweaks that had improved the defense.

General Manager Brandon Beane has a chance to bolster the group before Tuesday afternoon’s deadline and games against the Jets and Dolphins offer chances to keep building confidence over the next two weeks. Those things could help because the real tests of the Bills defense won’t come for some time.

#2787. ‘Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics

'Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Jaylen Brown was asked Sunday whether he and Jayson Tatum had spoken since the former teammates addressed their relationship during the preseason.

Does he plan to approach Tatum before Tuesday night's game at Xfinity Mobile Arena?

"I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said. "We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So it's nothing to talk about. Let's check the ball up."

After months of public comments, documentaries and questions about how their partnership ended, the basketball will finally take over.

Brown will face Boston for the first time since the Celtics traded him to Philadelphia for Paul George and four future draft assets in July. He spent his first 10 NBA seasons in Boston, played nine alongside Tatum and helped the Celtics win the 2024 championship, earning Finals MVP honors.

Tuesday's 8 p.m. game on NBC will also bring together the top two teams in the Eastern Conference. The Sixers are 9-2. Boston, riding a three-game winning streak, is 8-2 and sits a half-game behind Philadelphia.

"Another good opportunity for our team to be able to show what we're made of," Brown said. "I'm looking forward to it. Big-time matchup, two heavyweights in the East. Let's get it."

Brown has not hidden his appreciation for Boston, even as more has emerged about the deterioration of his relationship with Tatum and the organization.

"I love Boston," he said Sunday. "Boston's a great city. A lot of people I developed relationships with, you know what I mean? But I'm just focused on what's in front of me right now. And that's the most important thing."

He also acknowledged everything that accompanies an abrupt end to a decade with one organization.

"Decisions were made," Brown said. "It's life. It's business. Move on. It's OK. … It's emotions. You've got to pack up and move your stuff. Your family's got to pack up and move. But it's life. It's happened to numerous amounts of people, myself included.

"So I just look forward to being able to build with my team over here, trying to make the best of my situation."

Brown faced the Celtics during the preseason, but Tuesday will be the first meeting that counts. He said he did not know whether that would introduce emotions that were absent during the exhibition schedule.

"We'll see how I feel when we get out there," Brown said. "As of now, I've got no emotion toward nothing. So I'm just ready to go."

Tatum was similarly restrained after Boston's 117-97 victory over Milwaukee on Sunday.

"It's another game on the schedule," Tatum said. "It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one."

Tatum called the Sixers "an incredible group" with a "great coaching staff," but declined to add to the discussion surrounding his relationship with Brown.

"Drama gets clicks and views," he said. "That's not my thing." CBS Sports reported Tatum's full comments Sunday night.

Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla was even more concise.

"It'll be fun," Mazzulla said. "It'll be a good atmosphere."

Brown is not the only centerpiece of the July deal who will face his former team.

George has settled quickly into Boston's lineup, averaging 20.4 points and supplying the high-volume outside shooting the Celtics have long prioritized. He scored 27 points and made five three-pointers Sunday as Boston beat Milwaukee for its third consecutive victory.

The Celtics have not needed George to duplicate everything Brown provided. He has fit alongside Tatum, Derrick White and Boston's returning core as another willing shooter and versatile defender.

Tatum is averaging 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists. His playmaking has been especially important for a team that replaced Brown's downhill pressure with more shooting and ball movement.

Boston enters Tuesday ranked third in offensive rating and fourth in defensive rating. It is one of two NBA teams currently inside the top five on both ends of the floor.

The Celtics have also made 15.6 three-pointers per game, the second-highest average in the league. They set an NBA Cup record by hitting 24 against Charlotte on Friday, then made 18 more Sunday in Milwaukee.

That presents a clear challenge for a Sixers defense that has generally performed well but has occasionally surrendered clean perimeter looks after committing extra help toward the ball. Tatum, George, White, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser can all punish late rotations.

The Sixers have reached 9-2 without depending upon the same formula every night.

Tyrese Maxey leads them at 26.9 points per game. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists while shooting 47.7 percent from the field and 39.2 percent from three. Joel Embiid and LeBron James have supplied scoring, passing and defensive flexibility around them.

Brown has repeatedly described the team as unfinished despite its record.

"From our perspective, it's been some growing pains for sure, even though we've been able to win," he said. "The result, we're not so much fixated on the result. It's more so about the process, and we've got to improve our process and our mentality to creating a winning environment."

Boston should provide the clearest early measure of that process.

The Celtics play considerably slower than the Sixers, but their half-court execution has been more efficient. Philadelphia will want to create turnovers and run before Boston can set its defense. The Celtics will attempt to control the pace, generate three-pointers and make the Sixers execute against a defense that has yet to allow an opposing player to score 30 points this season.

There is also the unavoidable Brown matchup. Boston could use Tatum, George and White against him at different points, giving the Celtics several defenders capable of absorbing his drives without immediately sending help.

Nick Nurse expects Brown to bring something extra, even if Brown has publicly downplayed the emotional component.

"It's going to be very different for him," Nurse said. "I think probably a little bit of emotion in there, too, but also I think he's going to be very motivated to play."

Boston's rotation is healthy entering the matchup. Two-way guard Devin Carter is out because of an illness.

Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti remain out for the Sixers. Adem Bona could return after missing Sunday's contest.

The betting market views the matchup as essentially a toss-up. Monday afternoon listings had the spread moving between Boston minus-1.5 and Philadelphia minus-1.5, depending on the sportsbook, with the total at 215.5.

That fits the larger picture. Philadelphia owns the East's best record. Boston has the conference's strongest point differential and has outscored opponents by 10.7 points per game.

The surrounding conversation will center on Brown and Tatum until the opening tip. Brown does not intend to contribute any ceremonial small talk.

"He's on his side," Brown said. "I'm on my side."

#2784. John Harbaugh on trade deadline approach: If you put it on a scale, now outweighs the future

There have been a number of big moves on the trade front over the last couple of weeks as teams with eyes on competing for the Super Bowl have made big swings to improve their chances.

The Giants have made one significant trade and the move to add quarterback J.J. McCarthy in the wake of Jaxson Dart’s torn ACL has worked out well thus far. The team is 5-2-1 and in first place in the NFC East, which has led to a lot of speculation about whether there are more moves to come ahead of Tuesday’s 4 p.m. ET deadline.

While many expected the Giants to be better in John Harbaugh’s first season, that standing might find them a little further along than anticipated and Harbaugh was asked about how the team will weigh a short-term move against the long view of team building.

“Very true, very important, and yet you want to do everything you can do to make your team as strong as you can right now, because we’re in the now, and we’re told to live in the moment, be where our feet are planted, concern ourselves with today, but that’s not at the expense of tomorrow or just prudent planning,” Harbaugh said, via a transcript from the team. “I think we just have to look at each situation, and just weigh it out in terms of, okay, what’s the cost? What’s the benefit? And is it worth it? Is it going to benefit us? Is it a good thing for the Giants, and for the organization, and the team? So, I would say that the now weighs more important than the future, if you’re going to put it on a scale, and kind of go from there.”

People like to talk about championship windows, but they don’t always open and close on a prescribed schedule and the Giants will have to decide if it makes sense to try to widen their current one in the next few hours.

#2783. F1 makes final call on Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid Middle East situation

Formula 1 has confirmed that end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead as scheduled.

The final two rounds of the 2026 season in Qatar (29 November) and Abu Dhabi (6 December) had been shrouded in uncertainty due to the conflict in the Middle East. Races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier this season were cancelled, though Bahrain did fulfil its event with a one-off race in Malaysia in October.

F1 did have the historic Imola circuit as a back-up contingency plan for 6 December, with preliminary grandstands being built in and around the track site in the Emilia Romagna region of Italy.

However, given logistical and freight plans, The Independent understands that F1 has now told Imola to stand down. Qatar and Abu Dhabi will conclude the campaign as planned as part of one final triple-header, starting in Las Vegas on 21 November.

An F1 spokesperson added: "We are very grateful for the support and collaboration with the promoter and government in Imola and the region. If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority."

F1 added that all 11 teams are supportive of concluding the season as planned.

The final round of the MotoGP season took place in Qatar – at the same circuit in Lusail, just outside Doha – over the weekend without a hitch, though Yamaha did withdraw from the event pre-race. Nineteen riders also penned a letter expressing their wish not to race in Qatar, but both races were held as planned.

Previous UK travel guidance during the height of the US/Israel-Iran conflict this year advised against "all but essential" travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. However, that has since been lifted, with tension in the region cooling in recent weeks.

That being said, the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) does state that the "broader security context" in the Middle East "carries a risk of sudden escalation, potential flight cancellations and airspace disruptions."

Both F1 chief Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem have insisted in recent weeks that the Middle Eastern races will take place as planned, barring any sudden re-escalation of hostilities in the region. Ben Sulayem re-affirmed that commitment with a post on Instagram on Tuesday.

Moto GP finished their season in Qatar on Sunday (Reuters)

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, whose team clinched the constructors' championship in Brazil last weekend, a week after Kimi Antonelli won the drivers' title, had backed the sport to make the right call.

"Stefano and Mohammed have been pretty clear about the situation that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there are travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making," Wolff said.

"So not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion, and I'm fully with that.

"I think that if [MotoGP] riders stand up, who know nothing geopolitically about what's going on, but have an audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value. But I would have done the same as MotoGP management has done. You want to ride or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. It's as simple as that, and everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect that.

"Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, few weeks, and Stefano has his finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous and we would get that feedback, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. So that's why I'm following their guidance."

F1 has raced at Abu Dhabi, which has held the season finale for over a decade, since 2009 and Qatar since 2021.
