#2781. Celtics vs. Sixers has everything a great NBA rivalry needs…and now we’re adding Tatum and Brown

Sports rivalries rule. I grew up during the early-2000s Red Sox-Yankees battles. I'll never forget swinging from the absolute heartbreak of Aaron Boone's home run in 2003 to complete euphoria the following October, when the Sox cowboyed up, erased a 3-0 deficit and finally broke the curse.

I also got to experience the Celtics-Lakers rivalry returning to the NBA Finals in 2008 and 2010, when the animosity between the teams and their fans felt almost as important as the basketball itself. Those games were appointment television, and I'm still fiending for another Celtics-Lakers Finals.

LOS ANGELES – DECEMBER 25: Kobe Bryant #24 of the Los Angeles Lakers gets into an argument with Paul Pierce #34 and Kevin Garnett #5 of the Boston Celtics during their game at Staples Center on December 25, 2008 in Los Angeles, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2008 NBAE (Photo by Noah Graham/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

The NBA has produced some incredible rivalries throughout its history, but it feels like fewer of them have much staying power anymore. Players are constantly switching teams, contenders fall apart and yesterday's bitter enemies become tomorrow's podcast guests. Sometimes we're told two teams are rivals simply because the league scheduled them on Christmas or they're playing during Rivals Week, presented by Amazon Web Services. Because nothing screams genuine hatred like a comprehensive cloud computing platform.

Anyway, the Boston Celtics play the Philadelphia 76ers tonight.

In the lead-up, I've been thinking about what makes a great NBA rivalry and how many of those ingredients are present in the current relationship between Boston and Philadelphia. The more I thought about it, the more convinced I became that we're watching one of the league's oldest rivalries return to something resembling its best form.

Joel Embiid famously declared back in 2018 that Celtics-Sixers wasn't much of a rivalry because Boston kept beating Philadelphia. Eight years and one particularly painful playoff series later, I think it's worth revisiting his assessment.

I've settled on four criteria for evaluating a proper NBA rivalry, and Boston and Philadelphia are about to receive their entirely unofficial rivalry report card.

(Original Caption) Bill Russell of the Celtics turns a deaf ear on Wilt Chamberlain of the 76ers and has to be restrained by referee John Vanak away from Chamberlain.

You can't manufacture decades of bad blood, and Boston and Philadelphia have enough to fill a small museum. Ideally one with separate entrances for fans of each team.

The Celtics and Sixers have met in 23 playoff series, more than any other pairing in NBA history. Boston holds a 15-8 advantage, with some of basketball's greatest players participating in the ongoing effort to make the other franchise miserable.

It started with Bill Russell and Wilt Chamberlain, when Boston spent much of the 1960s blocking Wilt's path to a championship. Philadelphia finally broke through in 1967, ending the Celtics' run of eight consecutive titles.

Then came Larry Bird and Julius Erving, and an entirely new generation of reasons for the cities to dislike each other. The teams met in four Eastern Conference finals during the 1980s, splitting them 2-2. The 1981 series was particularly ridiculous, with Boston overcoming a 3-1 deficit and winning the final three games by a combined five points. Five!

And, of course, there was the infamous fight between Bird and Dr. J on November 9, 1984, which just celebrated its 42nd anniversary. Bird had already scored 42 points when things got ugly in the third quarter, with Moses Malone restraining him as Erving landed several punches.

Erving later explained his attitude toward playing Boston rather succinctly: "I don't care if it's your mother, you're not supposed to get along." I appreciate that level of commitment to the rivalry. Erving family dinners must have been interesting.

At that time, Philadelphia even had a player nicknamed the Boston Strangler. Andrew Toney earned the name by repeatedly torching the Celtics, including a 34-point performance in Game 7 of the 1982 Eastern Conference finals that sent Boston home.

Imagine being so consistently good at ruining another team's season that people start calling you the Boston Strangler. I'd have that printed on my business cards.

The beauty of this history is that it never really goes away. The players change, coaches come and go, and special-edition uniforms occasionally make us nauseous, but the relationship survives.

For a younger Celtics fan, tonight might be their first real introduction to the rivalry. Meanwhile, somewhere in Philadelphia, there's probably a grandfather who still refuses to allow anyone named Larry into his house.

What a time to get involved. There's nearly eighty years of basketball history waiting for you, and both teams have recently supplied plenty of new material.

For a long time, Boston fans had a pretty comfortable relationship with Philadelphia.

Remember Embiid's assessment from 2018? Following another loss to Boston, he famously said, "This is not a rivalry…they always kick our ass."

He wasn't wrong. Boston eliminated Philadelphia in six consecutive playoff meetings between 1985 and 2023.

The most memorable recent example came in 2023, when Jayson Tatum scored 51 points in Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals, setting the NBA's Game 7 scoring record at the time. Celtics fans celebrated while Sixers fans contemplated another year of trusting the process.

After Boston built a 3-1 series lead in the first round, Philadelphia won three straight games and completed the comeback with a 109-100 victory at TD Garden. Before that series, Boston had been 32-0 when leading a playoff series 3-1. Philadelphia had never overcome that deficit in 18 previous attempts.

For Celtics fans, it was a miserable way to end a season already defined by uncertainty surrounding Tatum's Achilles recovery. The Sixers, who'd spent years being reminded of their playoff failures against Boston, finally got to celebrate on the parquet.

And that's precisely what this rivalry needed, however gut-wrenching it is to admit. A rivalry becomes a lot less interesting when one team wins every meaningful matchup. Eventually, the winning side starts treating the opponent like a routine trip to the barber shop.

Philadelphia's comeback changed the dynamic.

Sixers fans now have a recent series in which their team delivered one of the most painful postseason defeats in Boston's history. On the flip side, Celtics fans can point to decades of superiority, but that doesn't make the most recent result any less irritating.

Both fan bases have something to bring up and something they'd desperately prefer the other forget.

I'm stopping short of an A because I'd like to see the teams trade a few more meaningful blows before declaring this an entirely balanced postseason feud. Preferably with Boston getting the next one.

We've spent an extraordinary amount of time discussing the relationship between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown since Boston traded Brown to Philadelphia.

At this point, the alleged beef has been stirred, sautéed, broiled, slow-cooked and served with several unnecessary side dishes. I'm sure a script is in the works to turn the story into a limited series.

The latest round of questions came this week as the former teammates prepared to face each other for the first time. Brown told CelticsBlog's Bobby Manning that the two had nothing to discuss before tipoff, while Tatum has continued emphasizing that he'd rather focus on basketball.

Tatum and Brown spent nine seasons together in Boston. They became perennial All-Stars, reached two NBA Finals and won a championship together in 2024. Whatever their relationship looks like today, I'd rather celebrate what they accomplished than spend another afternoon interpreting Brown's cryptic comments.

PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – APRIL 24: Jayson Tatum #0 and Jaylen Brown #7 of the Boston Celtics look on against the Philadelphia 76ers during game three of the Eastern Conference first round playoffs at Xfinity Mobile Arena on April 24, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Celtics defeated the 76ers 108-100. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Besides, the actual basketball matchup is much more enjoyable to dream about.

Will they guard each other? If they do, how much does their familiarity help? They've spent almost a decade practicing together, studying film together and learning how to attack defenses alongside one another. They know each other's habits, preferred spots and tendencies better than most opponents ever could.

Does that make defending each other easier, or do two players with that much shared experience become even more difficult to predict?

And somehow LeBron James has managed to find his way into this episode, too. At this point, we're approaching Avengers-level crossover territory.

LeBron spent years tormenting Boston during his Cleveland and Miami tenures. Now he's wearing a Sixers jersey alongside Brown, Embiid and Maxey, as though Philadelphia deliberately assembled a collection of Boston's greatest supervillains.

Meanwhile, Paul George is enjoying an excellent start in Boston after two difficult seasons with Philadelphia. His ability to operate alongside Tatum has been one of the Celtics' most encouraging early developments, and he'll have his own familiar faces waiting on the other side tonight.

There are enough connections here to keep the NBA's broadcast crew occupied for several hours. I'm just hoping we spend most of that time discussing how these players might actually compete against each other.

This might be the most important ingredient of all.

You can have decades of history and a roster full of former teammates, but the rivalry loses some appeal when one team is spending March counting down the days until its season ends.

The best NBA rivalries have stakes. Both teams need to be good enough that beating the other feels meaningful, preferably with a legitimate chance they'll meet again when the games matter most.

Through the first few weeks of the 2026-27 season, Boston and Philadelphia have certainly held up their ends of that arrangement.

The Sixers enter tonight at 9-2, sitting atop the Eastern Conference. Boston is right behind them at 8-2, having won three straight games, including Sunday's 117-97 victory over Milwaukee.

Philadelphia has quickly found success with its shiny new roster. Brown is averaging more than 22 points per game, while Maxey continues to be a nightmare for opposing defenses. Embiid remains an enormous problem whenever he's healthy, and LeBron gives the Sixers an ageless playmaker who has spent a good chunk of his life learning how to beat Boston.

The Celtics have started impressively despite undergoing significant changes themselves.

Tatum has returned to playing at an All-NBA level following his Achilles injury. George has fit beautifully alongside him, and Boston's supporting cast is beginning to settle into its new responsibilities. Joe Mazzulla has even started hugging people during games, a sign that either things are going well or the end times are near.

Tonight will be our first regular-season opportunity to see how these particular rosters match up.

Boston has to contend with Maxey's speed and Embiid's presence inside. Brown and George could find themselves defending one another, while Tatum's developing partnership with George faces one of its toughest tests yet.

There's plenty to examine beyond the inevitable pregame questions about who plans to shake whose hand.

And while I don't want to get ahead of myself ten games into the season, it's difficult to look at these rosters without imagining another playoff meeting in the near future.

If that happens, tonight could be the beginning of another particularly memorable chapter in a rivalry that already has a lot of unforgettable ones.

The history is there, Philadelphia has finally given Boston a reason to seek revenge, and the player storylines have somehow become more complicated than the plot of an HBO drama.

What we haven't seen is how all of that translates onto the court with these particular rosters.

Maybe tonight ends up being an ordinary basketball game. It's certainly possible Tatum and Brown exchange a quick handshake, everybody behaves like responsible adults, and the teams play 48 minutes without providing a single controversial quote.

At this point, that would probably be healthy for everyone involved.

Personally, I'm hoping for an excellent game with a little competitive nastiness. I wouldn't mind seeing Pritchard or Scheierman give Embiid a hard time after an inevitable flop. Maybe Anfernee Simons will have words for the Celtics coaching staff after burying a three in front of their bench.

After years of Boston getting the better of this rivalry, Philadelphia finally has something to brag about. I can't think of a better way to welcome the rivalry back than having the two teams actually play each other.

Just preferably with the Celtics winning.

#2780. Tuesday Miami Dolphins Thoughts With The Earl

You know, I understand that this season is about growth, development, and resetting the outlook. But is it too much to ask to get one game of complimentary football from this team? Yet another frustrating loss when one side of the ball shows up, but the other does not. Here's what I saw.

I can really call them, can't I? The Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins had two of the league's worst defenses coming into this game. I figured there would be a shootout, or at least a higher-scoring affair. Yet the game featured fewer than 500 total yards of offense and only 28 total points. The Lions averaged 29 PPG coming into this contest, scoring less than 20 points only once, and that was against the league's best defense, the Vikings. They averaged 6 yards per play before this game. Yet, the Miami Dolphins defense limited the Lions to 19 points and 4.6 yards per play. The Lions gained over 100 fewer yards than their per-game average for the season. For the 1st time all season, the pass defense allowed less than a 70% completion percentage. Goff was limited to 6.8 YPA, and he did not throw a TD. He was sacked 3 times. Rookie Chris Johnson got an INT. Not only that, but the run defense showed up again. The Lions gained 102 yards, but 25% of it came on 2 misdirection plays. Jahmyr Gibbs has been the league's most dominant weapon thus far this season, and he eventually found the end zone. But he was limited to 74 yards on 20 carries and no catches on 1 target. That's a 3.7 YPC average, and that's WITH 2 runs of 10+ yards. This was a terrible matchup for the Dolphins, but they stepped up in a big way.

The offense picked a bad time to be absent. The Lions had allowed 300+ yards in every game but one so far, and that was to the offensively challenged Vikings. They were fairly decent in run defense, although I suspected that was due to lack of volume. They score so much that teams abandon the run. The Dolphins had 21 rushing attempts, which is a little below their standard. Gordon ran fairly well when he got an opening. However, the story is that Willis had 2 scrambles for 7 yards. The stat itself isn't as striking as watching them happen. Willis is a dynamic runner, and we have seen him make big plays with his legs this season. But in the past 2 games, he has been reluctant to run. He has been on the injury report the past few weeks with a groin injury, but was listed as a full participant. It was obvious that the injury, or maybe something else, is hampering him. He ran slowly and lumbering, not at all like what we have seen from him. That doesn't excuse the INT, which was a bad decision. But it can explain why he can't escape pressure like he normally does, and why he ran the way I would have out there. I know fans hate excuses, but anyone who has ever dealt with a groin injury understands. You may feel fine walking around. But the moment you have to run and put forth effort, it's very painful, and you can't do it. It can affect everything, including throwing mechanics. Even with that, Willis had good moments. I don't want to make this about whether he is good enough, but as long as he is limited, the offense will be limited. I honestly wouldn't mind if they sat him for a while until he is healthy. In the past 2 games, he played at a higher level, and I believe that if he were 100% on Sunday, the Dolphins could have won. Well… there were other issues too.

Dirty laundry as far as the eye could see. Officiating in the league has been bad this season and too often, the guy sin stripes have been too visible. This game was no exception as there were a combined 20 accepted penalties. This isn't a "blame the refs" post though. The Dolphins were just bad in this regard. There was a huge pass play to Kevin Coleman Jr. that came back due to a holding penalty. Several drives had crushing penalties that put the offense way behind the sticks. This team doesn't have the talent to overcome problems like excessive penalties. To invoke the old Flores trope, those issues are the "takes no talent" stuff that should be improving. If I was Hafley, I would have those guys puking their guts out running gassers back and forth to the TNT wall for those penalties. It needs to stop.

THERE YOU ARE! You were hiding all along, and we thought you had disappeared. But you came back. I'm, of course, talking about the offensive line we have come to know and hate over the years. Willis was sacked 3 times – I saw 2 of them – and those, I would argue, are due to his inability to escape like he wants to. But he was under assault all game long. He had several where he was flushed from the pocket and couldn't find an open pass catcher. Austin Jackson was particularly atrocious, and Slowik's decision to have him go one-on-one with a premier pass rusher defies logic. That hurt the game plan and may have killed any trade value he had. Paul seemed to have a decent day, but everyone else struggled, and it was pretty rough to watch.

Will Kacmarek had a rough game. He nullified the huge pass play to Coleman. Then he had a terrible sequence in the 2nd half where he had a false start on 2nd down, then dropped a 3rd-down pass that would have converted. The Dolphins converted the fake punt play right after that, so they stayed on the field. But that was a bad stretch. He was known as a limited but reliable receiver in college. Can't have those big drops with limited opportunities.

Both Douglas and Coleman look like keepers. Douglas is the big-time playmaker, but Coleman has stepped it up. He only had one target, but it was a huge play. Well, it should have been a huge play. Bell remains quiet, and concerns about his ability to create separation are growing. I remain firm in the belief that he is a big slot player. But right now, he isn't stepping up like his rookie counterparts.

Bradley Pinion had the best pass of the game for the Dolphins on the fake punt play. But the shanked punt gave the Lions great field position that led to points. The defense forced a FG, but it was a 40-yard FG. Imagine if the punt had been 45 yards instead of 25. If the same play sequence occurs, the Lions may be forced to kick a 60-yarder instead. Or perhaps they go for it on 4th-and-10. Or maybe they punt.

Not that it mattered, because the Dolphins took the ball, marched down the field, and attempted a FGto tie the game at halftime. Gonzalez doinked the kick off the upright. Now, that 6-point swing didn't necessarily affect the outcome. But look at that sequence of events. A shanked punt led to field position and 3 points from Detroit, giving them a 6-3 lead. What if they don't get those points because the Dolphins' defense steps up after a better punt? What if Gonzalez hits that FG and the Dolphins get a 3-point lead going into the half?

Again, it's little mistakes like the poor punt, missed FG, and penalties that can affect the margins, and the Dolphins have to win the margins to have a chance. I can be lenient with rookies like Kacmarek. But Gonzalez and Pinion are literally the oldest players on the Dolphins' field. That is simply unacceptable performance for those players. Gonzalez has had his 3rd call-up from the practice squad, and the team will have to decide whether to add him to the 53-man roster or let him walk. At this point, I would try out some young kickers and let them have a chance. Who cares if they miss or if they suck? It's about seeing what kind of gems the team can unearth. Maybe they find a stud kicker. Maybe not. But Gonzalez ain't it, and neither is Pinion. The Dolphins are 1-7. There is no use hanging on to old specialists that are underperforming.

The pass rush had its moments early, but disappeared late in the game. They need to keep up the pressure for a full 60 minutes.

Kaytron Allen had his first NFL carry and first NFL reception on Sunday. He dropped his run for a yard loss, but he had the play of the day on the fake punt. I think he should get more touches this season.

Jaylen Wright was a potentially healthy scratch. He missed some practice time because of a quad issue but tested it out during the pre-game. Some who saw his warm-up said he looked fine and could have played. I think he could be on the trade block, and with not much happening on the Jonathan Taylor front, teams may look for a much cheaper option if they need running back depth.

If Jackson still has a market, they need to make the move. It's time to move on. I get the idea of keeping him to help evaluate Willis or whatever. But it ain't working. Caedan Wallace… you're up.

As I mentioned at the beginning, this game was frustrating because one side of the ball can't play well enough to compliment the other. Perhaps the Dolphins can finally put it together against a reeling Colts team that has given up on the season and started trading off players.

#2778. Fantasy Football studs & duds Week 10 of 2026 NFL season

Back to four we go. With only two teams on a Week 9 bye, we had a reprieve. That's over in Week 10 as four teams have players that we need to replace in our fantasy football lineups.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Chicago Bears, Philadelphia Eagles, and Denver Broncos all have Week 10 bye weeks. All that we can do is move forward, as we know that the NFL changes like the wind. So, let's dig into some fantasy football studs and duds for Week 10.

#2777. Vikings' 17:28 time of possession was their lowest in franchise history

The Minnesota Vikings have played 1,064 games in the history of their franchise, which started in 1961. Before yesterday, they had never played a game in which they possessed the ball for less than 17 and a half minutes. Now they have.

The Vikings’ time of possession of 17:28 in Monday night’s 23-6 loss to the Bills was their lowest in franchise history.

The previous franchise low was 17:38, set in the NFC Championship Game after the 2000 season, when the Vikings lost to the Giants 41-0.

On Monday night, the Vikings’ offense could not stay on the field. The first quarter set the tone: They had three possessions, which were two three-and-outs and one possession on which they lost a fumble on the first play. Their longest possession of the night lasted 3:11, and on that possession they ran five plays, totaled just 10 yards, and punted.

The Vikings’ defense played well, but not so well that the Bills weren’t able to sustain some long drives, including three drives that took more than six minutes off the clock. The Bills gained 22 first downs; the Vikings gained just nine.

The Bills’ 42:32 time of possession was their second-best in franchise history, trailing only a 1989 game in which they possessed the ball for 42:53 and beat the Jets 34-3.

#2776. Where's the beef? First Tatum vs. Brown showdown could provide early scorecard

For the first time since they spent nine prolific seasons together, while rising to the top of the NBA, Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown will face off as opponents in the regular season.

The Boston Celtics (8-2) head to Philadelphia Tuesday, Nov. 10 to battle the 76ers (9-2), the team that acquired Brown in a July blockbuster trade. And with that comes the next chapter in a relationship that has at times became tense and uncomfortable.

Despite that, as the game approaches, both sides have been sure to down play any drama.

"It's nothing to talk about," Brown told reporters Sunday, Nov. 8. "I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side. Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so it's nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up."

Yet, now that we're three weeks into the 2026-27 season, it's a fair time to pose a couple questions.

One: is there a clear winner in the trade? And, two: will either team come to regret their choice?

At first glance, it's like a rare case where the move benefitted both sides; entering Monday night, these were the top two teams in the Eastern Conference. The Celtics were leading the NBA in net rating (+11.6), and the Sixers have been seamlessly sharing the ball and rank third in assist-to-turnover ratio (2.01).

It's necessary, however, to point out a few caveats here. The sample size remains rather small and, entering Monday night, the Celtics had played the NBA's easiest strength of schedule (.396), according to ESPN; Philadelphia's, by comparison, ranked 20th (.476).

To be clear, neither of these points are disqualifying, but both teams – Boston in particular – need to demonstrate that they can sustain these levels over time and against the league's better competition.

The most positive sign for both teams is that the issues that originally forced the divorce in the first place don't appear to have carried over.

Dating back to their first seasons as stars in Boston, the narrative surrounding Tatum and Brown was that they were not optimal fits. They both excel with the ball in their hands, and both can create their own shot with ease. That often led to a disjointed offense, where they often took turns scoring in isolation.

In Boston, Paul George, whom Philadelphia sent to Boston in the Brown trade, has been nothing but steady. He has acknowledged that his sole role is to be complementary to Tatum, and his 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds and 4.1 assists per game are more than sufficient.

In Philadelphia, Brown's numbers are a little better (22.3/6.7/4.0), but he has directly addressed the dynamics of his new team, saying point guard Tyrese Maxey "has been leading the way for sure" and that the Sixers are "his team," referring to Maxey.

Brown has been more provocative in his public comments about any feud between he and Tatum. He recently posted an emoji of a blue hat – which is another way to say cap, or slang that someone is being dishonest – to a video on social media in which Tatum said he was caught off guard by the July trade. Even in a recent comment that began with praise for Tatum, Brown snuck in a sly jab.

"I think he's right," Brown said Oct. 24. "There's no beef. Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things, he's a hell of a basketball player, he got a great (public relations) team. There's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chops and some gravy, and he should stay ready at all times."

In their first meeting as opponents, a preseason game Oct. 16 in which Brown did not play, both players warmed up on opposite sides of the floor and did not acknowledge each other, at least not publicly.

"All of y'all kind of saw us grow up and everything that we accomplished," Tatum said recently. "... Like, how many people play in this league and never went to the Finals? We went twice and won a championship. So it should be more about that. This ain't no (expletive) Shaq and Kobe. It's not about that.

"It should be more praise, and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but that's not my thing."

This all raises one last question, about whether it's fair to criticize players on the same team for not being friends off the floor. Just because their work is televised and just because they're paid handsomely does not mandate that they be forced into any sort of deeper bond we fans and media seemingly expect out of athletes. At the end of the day, they are – at least in professional terms – merely employees just like you and I. And just like you and I may have colleagues with whom we might not necessarily align, these players are entitled just the same.

This trade was not executed because of any perceived fractured friendship. The Celtics clearly prioritized one player's skill set over another's, and they made a difficult choice, one that does not come without some risk. They wanted to divest away from having two max contracts.

Tuesday night's game is just the next logical step, nothing more.

#2774. 3 messiest NBA breakups, including Jaylen Brown & Jayson Tatum

Breakups happen in life. They happen in the NBA, and we get to see two former teammates square off this Tuesday night when Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown face off for the first time as opponents.

This isn't something new in the NBA, and we've seen it plenty of times. One guy wants to be the lone star on the team, or a dynamic duo just can't get over the top and win a championship. It can get messy real quick; shots through the media, and fans start taking sides.

What was the messiest breakup in NBA history? Here are three divorces that caused the most drama.

MORE: Giannis Antetokounmpo fires back at Doc Rivers' 'uncoachable' comments

May 29, 2012; San Antonio, TX, USA; Oklahoma City Thunder players Russell Westbrook (0), and Derek Fisher (37), and Kendrick Perkins (5), and James Harden (13) and Kevin Durant (35) on the court during a timeout in game two of the Western Conference finals of the 2012 NBA playoffs against the San Antonio Spurs at the AT&T Center. the Spurs won 120-111. Mandatory Credit: Soobum Im-Imagn Images

Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook were one of the most fun duos we've ever seen. They played together on the Oklahoma City Thunder for nine seasons. Durant and Westbrook were the faces of an exciting young team, and they made the 2012 NBA Finals but fell to the Miami Heat in five games.

This duo lost to the Golden State Warriors in the 2016 Western Conference Finals, and that's where the drama started. Durant left for greener pastures in Golden State, and the divorce was official.

Westbrook was wondering, "They beat us, and you joined the enemy?" That's exactly what Durant did, and he went on to win two championships with DubNation. Westbrook never got his ring, but he won MVP in 2016-17, averaging a triple-double.

June 12, 2002; East Rutherford, NJ; The Lakers Kobe Bryant holds up the Championship trophy along with teammate Shaquille O'Neal who holds up his third MVP trophy. Mandatory Credit: Michael J. Terola/Abury Park Press-USA TODAY NETWORK

The Kobe Bryant–Shaquille O'Neal divorce was one of the most dramatic and bitter breakups in sports history. A duo that had so much success together, but that success ultimately led them to go their separate ways.

They won three championships in a row from 2000-2002 with the Los Angeles Lakers, and O'Neal was traded to the Miami Heat in 2004. They each wanted to be "The Guy" and that's what they got. It led to wild raps from Shaq, with both taking shots at each other through the media and outright hate.

They patched things up in a one-on-one interview in 2018, and many are glad they did. Bryant tragically passed away in 2020, and you could see how much it impacted O'Neal. This duo will be be remembered forever for their dominance, but also for their breakup. It was must-see TV every time they faced off.

Apr 28, 2026; Boston, Massachusetts, USA; Boston Celtics forward Jayson Tatum (0) and guard Jaylen Brown (7) warm up before the start of the game against the Philadelphia 76ers in game five of the first round of the 2026 NBA Playoffs at TD Garden. Mandatory Credit: David Butler II-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

This is the freshest breakup, and it's one of the more passive-aggressive breakups we've seen. It was clear both players wanted their own team and to carve their own path. Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum won a championship together with the Boston Celtics in 2024 but always dealt with the "whose team is it" question.

That question led to a divorce that will inch toward closure when they battle for the first time. The Celtics chose Tatum over Brown, and it will be a few years before we know if it's the right decision.

Does Brown blame Tatum for the breakup? It sure seems like it, and he's said he hasn't talked to Tatum since the Celtics traded him to the Philadelphia 76ers for Paul George. All eyes will be on this matchup, and it should be a great tilt.

#2773. Ugly wins cannot save these underperforming Cowboys

The Dallas Cowboys found a way to win a football game on Sunday, but the mood across Cowboys Nation remained surprisingly somber. Losing this matchup would have been absolutely devastating, for all intents and purposes ending their season. Falling four games behind the New York Giants in the loss column is a hole simply too deep to climb out of, especially with a brutal stretch of schedule coming soon. This made Sunday's win super important, yet at the same time, it offers very little reassurance.

The Cowboys may have secured the victory, but once again, what they showed on the field revealed a team that continues to make life incredibly difficult for themselves, even when facing bad opponents. The game looked eerily similar to the prior week's letdown against the Arizona Cardinals. In a game where it felt like the Cowboys were in complete control, they chose to play around rather than put their opponent away, eventually leading to another shocking moment where they suddenly found themselves trailing late in the fourth quarter.

The most troubling part of this situation is how familiar this has become. Over the last two weeks, the team has reproduced that exact gut-wrenching feeling that gave fans major anxiety during those consecutive nail-biting weeks against Baltimore and Houston earlier in the year.

It's the same story. They begin slowly, eventually start to get their act together to build a lead, and then watch it gradually wither away. Fortunately, against the Texans earlier in the season, they were able to escape with a victory thanks to a game-winning drive on the back of a clutch fourth-down conversion. But down in Rio, they weren't so lucky. Instead of punching the ball into the end zone with just a handful of seconds left on the clock, the offense sputtered and settled for a field goal, allowing the Ravens to make the game-winning play themselves.

The heartbreaking finish left fans playing the what-if game and asking why the Cowboys keep letting this happen. Fast forward a month later, and the exact same scenario is unfolding all over again, except this time it is happening against even worse teams.

The Arizona debacle last week was an absolute horror show. The Cardinals did not score a single point until late in the first half and were down by two touchdowns in the fourth quarter before things completely fell apart. The most infuriating part is that the offense had the opportunity to run out the clock if they could have secured one measly first down late in the game. They failed, the Cardinals mounted a comeback, and fans everywhere watched their team collapse.

On Sunday, it looked like it was happening again. It was painful to watch the offense struggle so mightily to score touchdowns against a poor Colts defense. Up until the final 70 seconds of the game, the offense had only found the end zone twice, and it required a clutch fourth-down grab by Jake Ferguson and a huge coverage breakdown for CeeDee Lamb's big touchdown right at the end of the first half.

Strangely enough, clutch fourth-down execution from Ferguson and Lamb exploding for over 180 receiving yards were identical saving graces in each of their close victory against their AFC South opponents this year. Imagine if those two things didn't happen? The Cowboys would be sitting at an abysmal 2-7 with a completely dead season, and the entire fanbase would be stressing over how the New York Jets are about to inherit a top-five draft pick courtesy of the front office.

All of this is to say that the Cowboys are an absolute mess right now. Are they still within striking distance of the NFC East crown? Sure, but we must remind ourselves that the schedule gets significantly tougher over the second half of the season, and this group has not beaten a single opponent with a winning record all year. In fact, they are 1-5 against teams with a record of 3-6 or better. That is a scary statistic.

Of the final eight opponents left on the schedule, five currently boast winning records. The month of December looks particularly ominous, featuring a four-game stretch against teams who all currently have a winning record. The storm is coming.

For a team that struggles to put away struggling teams, anticipating how they will hold up against stronger opponents is frightening. This team shows zero signs of turning the corner or correcting their chronic mental lapses. Instead, they prefer to lollygag and repeatedly engage in unnecessary wild finishes.

All of this seems avoidable. They have to be better than this, but sadly, they just refuse to play like it. Hang on to your drama subscription because it won't be going away anytime soon.

#2771. Sixers return home for tough test against Celtics

It wasn't the smoothest win on Sunday, but the Sixers still held things together in the fourth quarter to beat the Bulls 127-121.

It takes Philadelphia to 9-2 on the season, and they're in for more of a challenge on Tuesday. Next, as they return from their road trip, they're taking on the team fighting them for the first spot in the East: the Boston Celtics.

As per usual, the Celtics are continuing their trend of being a top team on both ends of the floor. After ranking in the top four in both offensive and defensive rating last season, they're top four in both areas yet again this season and first in net rating at +11.6.

Jayson Tatum, in his first full season back from his Achilles injury, has started strong. As the clear leader of the offense, he's averaging 27.1 points, 6.0 rebounds and a big jump in assists to a career-high 7.8 per game. His usage percentage is higher than ever at 33.3, he's effectively creating more for others, and the Celtics are using him well by running him off screens and getting him attacking downhill.

Tatum's shot selection will be something else to be mindful of for the Sixers' defense. So far, he's cut down his three-pointers from at least 49 percent of his total field goal attempts in the last two seasons to 38.1, while using more attacks at the rim and mid-rangers.

If the Sixers' forwards can guard Tatum physically and Joel Embiid can stay spry with his interior rotations and rim protection, that will be key to building an advantage on Tuesday.

Of course, the personal storyline we have to focus on in this one is Jaylen Brown's first regular season contest against his former team. He's already had some choice words for his old team and running mate Tatum to keep things entertaining lately.

Brown is entering the game in a great rhythm as well. He was stellar yet again in the Sixers' win on Sunday, finishing with 29 points on 11-of-22 shooting, seven rebounds, four assists and a steal. Not to mention some important plays down the stretch to help lead the offense on a night the Sixers' defense looked tired.

On the flip side, this is also going to be Paul George's first game in Philadelphia since being dealt to the Celtics. And to his credit, he's playing great at both ends of the floor to start his tenure in Boston. Through nine games, George has averaged 20.4 points while shooting 42.5 percent from three on 8.1 attempts, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals per game, while playing excellent, versatile defense.

George will be another good matchup for Brown, LeBron James and Dean Wade as the Sixers' forwards switch across him and Tatum, and contesting George's three-point threat in particular will be key to complementing defense of Tatum inside.

With Adem Bona remaining out due to his back injury, we should continue seeing more of Jabari Walker as a smaller backup center. He played a season-high of 19 minutes and 13 seconds against the Bulls on Sunday, and played well again — just as he has since preseason. Walker finished with nine points on 4-of-8 shooting and 11 rebounds, including an impressive five offensive boards. He hustled hard, was an integral factor in the Sixers out rebounding the Bulls, and even hit a three-pointer for good measure.

The Celtics do have more size with two 7-footers in Neemias Queta and Mitchell Robinson as their top centers, though, so Walker is going to be stretched. It'll be interesting to see how he fares and competes physically to try and keep them in check on dives to the rim and go to work as a rebounder.

This matchup should be a great test for the Sixers' 20th-ranked offense overall. From Derrick White's elite defense in the backcourt, to Tatum and George disrupting on the wings and Queta and Robinson's rim protection. We've seen many flashes of just how dangerous the Sixers' new offense can be and lots of individual brilliance, whether it's LeBron's passing or Tyrese Maxey's electric scoring. But after a rough defeat against the Cavaliers on Friday and a shaky win against the Bulls, the Sixers are likely going to need a more consistent, balanced effort to beat the Celtics.

If the Sixers can handle Boston on Tuesday and the Raptors on Thursday, they'll be in good shape to strengthen their hold on the No. 1 seed this month. Because after that, the Sixers' schedule starts easing up with plenty of matchups against teams under .500 through the rest of November.

We've seen these Sixers take down several difficult opponents already. Let's see if they can do it again the Celtics.

So far, San Francisco has consistently been the best team in the league, and with better health, they'll be very hard to beat down the stretch. Overall, it's hard to ask for much more than what we've seen from them so far this season, but don't sleep on the other two teams in this division to make things interesting over the final two months of the season.

If you were asleep all offseason and didn't know the Bills made a change at head coach, you'd probably think this was just business as usual for Buffalo. In many ways, it has been, but it's been pretty impressive to see them pick up as nothing changed with the coaching staff. Quarterback Josh Allen is awesome, but the defense will once again define how their season ends. Right now, it hasn't been good enough, but they've kept winning anyway. Will a deadline move (or two) get that unit heading in the right direction? We shall see.

What's not to like about the Jaguars right now? They have three wins by 23 points or more, Trevor Lawrence is playing like a top-tier quarterback, and the defense continues to dominate, especially in the run game. This is an extremely well-rounded team that shouldn't be discounted because of the division they are in. This is a Super Bowl contender with a very good roster and coaching staff.

Coming into Sunday night, the Bears were off to their best start since 2012. All of that while missing quarterback Caleb Williams for three games and figuring out the defense along the way. The addition of Jeffery Simmons is huge, but it'll come down to whether they can start winning divisional games. They should be a Super Bowl favorite, but if they have one weakness, that is it. We'll see how things go coming out of the bye, because starting Thanksgiving, the road to finishing the regular season is a gauntlet.

The Lions are playing their best football in two seasons, and knock on wood, their defense is finally improving. Losing All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell was scary and a big blow to this team, but getting back both high-level safeties should help. The offense will ultimately dictate how far this group can go, but they are well-coached and have plenty of talent. Don't sleep on the Lions over the second half of the season.

The Bengals have been hard to figure out so far this year, mainly because of their slow starts. The talent is there, and the defense is better, but can they improve enough to chase down the Steelers for the AFC North title? A lot will come down to how much the defense improves over the last two months of the season. It's all in front of them, and with the Ravens fading fast, the road gets a little easier.

This season started as a disaster for Green Bay, but they've found a way to push through adversity and come out looking like a much better team on the other side. Quarterback Jordan Love is playing at a high level, and the defense has rounded into form, despite missing star pass rusher Micah Parsons. Existing in the NFC North is tough, and like the other three teams, there's going to be little margin for error down the stretch. The good news is, the Packers have plenty of experience pushing through to the postseason.

Mid-season Report Card Grade: B+Despite a slow start, mostly due to the offense, this is still a very good team that might have its best football ahead of it. The biggest issue has been Bo Nix's play. Without a step up, it's hard to imagine they'll be able to win the AFC. That said, with a step in the right direction, they are as dangerous as any team in the conference. Finding another playmaker on the offensive side of the ball should be a priority, so we'll see how it all plays out.

Their 5-0 start felt like a dream, but reality has hit over the last few weeks. The good news is that this is clearly a good team. The question remains whether or not they can ultimately win the division. This team desperately needs at least another pass catcher, but if they get into the playoffs, which they should, they'll be dangerous with the high-level experience of winning the big game.

Color me surprised that the Steelers have somehow been better under Mike McCarthy than they were in Mike Tomlin's final seasons. In many ways, their defense has carried the momentum. Still, credit goes to this offense, and especially 43-year-old quarterback Aaron Rodgers, for continuing to play at a high enough level. I'm still not sold that they can maintain this all season, but the last month they have looked like a very good team. We'll see if it lasts.

The defense is playing at a 1985 Chicago Bears level, but the offense is bottom three in most key statistical categories. Maybe a change at quarterback (although head coach Kevin O'Connell hasn't made it permanent) will make the difference, but the schedule ahead will be the ultimate test to show how good this team is as a whole. Adding a high-level running back will help, but without better quarterback play, their ceiling is limited.

In many ways, it's been a disastrous start to the season for the Rams, yet they come out of Week 9 above .500. Getting back Myles Garrett will be big, but the injuries they've suffered on the defensive side of the ball can't be ignored. If all goes well, the Rams and Seahawks will be fighting for a playoff spot, but this team has a long way to go to find enough consistency to live up to being heavy Super Bowl favorites. If they make the playoffs, it will likely be from a Wild Card spot, which is a tough ask for any team.

Are the Seahawks a good team? I believe they are. They have too much talent and too much already established for them to fall off completely. That said, they are in a tough division and conference, and so far this year, it's shown. The defense is still elite, but without better quarterback play, they are severely capped. All in all, it's been a disappointing start, but I expect to see them in the playoffs come January.

Count me as one of the people who didn't quite believe that John Harbaugh's presence would automatically make the Giants a good team. I was wrong, and I'm totally OK admitting that. Not only are they leading the NFC East, but they've done it starting three quarterbacks. Once Jaxson Dart was lost, it would have been easy to write them off, yet they've kept their pace and have played solid football along the way. The Giants aren't likely to be a big threat in the playoffs, but count this as a "one year ahead of schedule" kind of team, with plenty of upside moving forward.

Coming into the season, the Patriots were a favorite regression candidate. Despite a slow start, namely from quarterback Drake Maye, they've figured things out and look primed to at least push for a top Wild Card spot. The defense isn't quite as dominant as last year, but there's still plenty of time to get hot before the start of the playoffs. All in all, this is still a good team that should get better.

Raise your hand if you had the Browns as one of the worst teams in the league coming into the regular season. Most of us did, so it's OK. That's why they are one of three teams that earned an A+ in our Mid-season Report Cards. Quarterback is still a long-term question, but the fact that they are in the running for a playoff spot, despite trading Myles Garret,t speaks to the job that first-year head coach Todd Monken has done. Even better, they'll have a pair of first-round picks in next April's draft. No matter how the season ends, it's been a successful first half for the Browns.

Squandering away a 3-0 start would be hard to swallow for most teams, and although it's fair for anyone to be disappointed with the results since then, it's important to remember that the Raiders are a work in progress. Quarterback Kirk Cousins has been much better than expected, and their No. 1 overall pick hasn't even seen the field yet. They should possess enough cap flexibility to once again swing big next March, but the future should be bright as long as Fernando Mendoza is as good as his draft slot expects him to be.

Despite Jerry Jones' best efforts, his team simply hasn't been very good. After trading away Micah Parsons, they should have retool and committed to a new direction. Instead, they made multiple trades to replace him and still fielded one of the league's worst defenses. Even with their early-season struggles, they still have a fighter's chance to win a weakened NFC East. Even if they do, what's the overall ceiling for this season and beyond? This rudderless ship keeps acting out of desperation while ignoring reality.

It's been a nightmare start to the season for the Texans, and even if things have gotten better in recent weeks, there are still a lot of questions about this club's ability to make the playoffs. The good news is that C.J. Stroud has returned to his rookie form, but everything else around him has been an extreme disappointment. They'll have to go on an impressive run to get themselves back in the playoff race, which will likely be a Wild Card appearance.

Most teams would have been sunk after a 0-4 start, especially when that included losing your starting quarterback for multiple weeks. Instead, they've fought back, and because of the division they are in, they're right in the race. That said, the passing offense has been a big concern, and against better teams, they won't average over 200 yards per game. The continued question about this group is: what's the end goal? None of that has been answered through nine games.

After a big offseason, expectations were that the Panthers would take the next step after winning the NFC South with a below-.500 record. After an impressive start, the offense has taken a step back. The defense has been a disaster, and while some of that can be credited to injuries, something is still missing. They might still be the favorites for the division, but they have a long way to go before they are considered true contenders.

For complete transparency, I had the Saints as my NFC South winners heading into the season. Although that's still possible, a disappointing start was far from what I was expecting. Quarterback Tyler Shough continues to show he's the guy, but there's a lot around him that has been less than ideal. Owner Gale Benson has already said the leash will not be long for this regime if they can't win, so they need to start showing progress soon.

All things considered, the Falcons are having a better season than most expected, especially after bringing in a brand-new regime and making some changes. Quarterback Michael Penix has been up-and-down, but overall, I'd say the good has outweighed the bad with the offense. Luckily, they are right in the mix for the division, and you could make a good argument that they might have the best roster of any of the four teams in the division.

With Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley done for the year, the season has quickly gone from promising to a complete disaster. There was plenty of optimism for Jesse Minter's first year and for good reason. More concerning than an offense on their third- and fourth-quarterback is how poorly the defense continues to play. There's a lot to be determined this offseason with some of their core pieces, but this season is quickly slipping away.

All things considered, the Cardinals have been a thorn in the side of a few teams so far this season. Even in Year 1 of Mike LaFleur, they've shown signs of progress, which is about all you can ask for considering where they were heading into the season. Quarterback is the big question here, especially after trading Jacoby Brissett to the Ravens. How they finish out the season might directly impact how effectively they can fill that void in the draft. Either way, they've been better than expected through nine weeks.

Injuries have played their part in a disappointing start to the season. Still, this franchise's inability to surround its franchise quarterback with a good offensive line and proper weapons remains a big issue. Hey, I get it. Dan Quinn is a defensive-minded guy, but c'mon now. Quarterback Jayden Daniels has durability issues, but when he's played, he's looked pretty good. The issue in his development is that they've completely abandoned the under-center option. Washington's falloff last year was unfortunate, but so far, it's showing who they are compared to their impressive 2024 breakout campaign. That's just not an acceptable outcome.

Not cutting bait with Chris Ballard and/or Shane Steichen this past offseason proved to be a predictable mistake early in the season. Ownership changes can be tricky, but it's clear that Carlie Irsay-Gordon has her own vision for this team, and middling will no longer be tolerated. Instead of delaying the inevitable, they sold off veteran pieces and could ship more off before Tuesday's deadline. It's going to be a long rebuild for Indianapolis, but it's long overdue. It's just a shame they could have forecasted better before handing out big contracts to Daniel Jones and Alec Pierce.

Despite a similar record to last season, the Jets are clearly a better team than they were this time last season. That said, there's still a lot of close and end-game situations where they simply aren't finding a way to make it. General manager Darren Mougey has done an outstanding job of accumulating high first-round picks heading into next year's draft. Still, this coaching staff needs a thorough evaluation, especially if they decide to draft a quarterback with one of those picks.

Losing quarterback Jalen Hurts might have been the final nail in the coffin for the Eagles' season in 2026, but there have been plenty of issues with this group going back to last year. Similar to the end of the Doug Pederson era, the bottom has completely fallen out of this regime. We'll see what changes they make this offseason, but the good news is Philadelphia is built to fix this quickly. For now, 2026 is just an unmitigated disaster.

Hiring Robert Saleh with a struggling No. 1 overall pick at quarterback was always a gamble, and so far, that has not paid off. They've been close to winning a few games they've ultimately lost, but in general, this team is far behind where they should be. After trading their face of the franchise, Jeffery Simmons, to the Bears, there are serious questions about whether they'll need to tear it down again, and that will start at quarterback. No matter how you cut it, 2026 has been yet another disaster.

Heading into the season, everyone knew the Dolphins were in the beginning stages of an extensive rebuild. Even with a bad record, there's been some good in what Miami has done this season. It'll take a few offseasons for the plan to take shape, but frankly, they've had moments of looking better than some of the other teams on this list that are above them.

When the Chargers hired Jim Harbaugh in 2024, nobody could have expected that three seasons later they'd be the NFL's lone winless team. Unfortunately, that's where things stood for them at the beginning of November. We'll see if they move on from their refusal to sell, but they have a ton of issues to address this offseason. First, what the hell happened to quarterback Justin Herbert?

#2768. Charge want to be a pipeline for the Cavs: ‘We want the development to be in-house’

CLEVELAND — The G League matters more for team building than ever. Look no further than the Cleveland Cavaliers roster for proof.

Seven of the 14 players on standard deals for the Cavs have spent time in the G League. That number should jump to eight, with Khalifa Diop expecting to play with the Cleveland Charge some this year as well. Diop's inclusion would mean that over half the roster has spent time in the G League.

This is a change from where things were over a decade ago. The reasons for that are layered. Investment in the league, along with changes to the salary cap and the style of play, has all contributed to this.

"In the world of aprons and salary cap and all this, what better way to cultivate the next wave of people that can help fit into [an NBA] environment than this?" Charge head coach Eli Kell-Abrams said.

The Cavs have invested in the Charge over the last several seasons. The move from Canton to Cleveland has allowed them to use the Cavs' training facility. More recently, switching their home games to Cleveland Public Auditorium, along with refitting the building for basketball, speaks to the organization's commitment to the G League.

"We want the development to be in-house," Charge general manager Liron Fanan said. "The type of players that you now take on your G League team, you really take into consideration what Kenny [Atkinson] and his staff are looking for. What kind of player are they on and off the court? How can he fit our culture of the Cavs and what we're looking for? It's mainly guys that are willing to accept a role, willing to compete every day, work hard, put their head down, and be ready."

The Charge are looking to identify and develop role players who can specifically fit alongside the Cavs' core group. There are two skills that the Charge are looking to cultivate, knowing that they will translate to the next level.

"They're going to have to be defensively minded, and also able to make shots when you stand in the corner because you're not going to have the ball in your hands," Fanan said. "You're going to be that guy that comes off the bench for five minutes and tries to impact the game in those minutes. So, how ready are you? What's your mentality? The toughness and the willingness to just take a role. Those are the skills that we look at."

The Charge are trying to refine those skills with their two-way players. Riley Minix has proven to be a good shooter — Summer League notwithstanding — but shooting alone isn't going to allow him to become a rotation player. "He needs to get better [defensively]," Fanan said. "Can he really defend and switch at the NBA level? We saw a little bit of that, and we're seeing improvement. I think there needs to be a big jump this year."

Rookie two-way center Ernest Udeh Jr. has the potential to develop into a useful backup center. The Cavs like the motor, but there's a learning curve for bigs transitioning from college to the pros.

"He always plays hard, now for us, it's to get him better at understanding spacing," Fanan said. "Understanding guarding outside the perimeter, working with his hands better."

Success in the G League is different than the NBA. The Charge want to win games, but their goal is to ensure they're developing talent that can be used by the Cavs and other NBA teams. For them to continue doing that, they want to continue cultivating a culture that makes that possible.

"We're in a league that is sometimes not about the right stuff," Kell-Abrams said. "We want to be the group that relies on each other, that is about everybody else's success. That passed the ball in a league that doesn't."

The Charge open their season at home on Tuesday night against the Motor City Cruise.

#2766. Tommy Doman forced a fumble in his first look on kickoffs

Buffalo Bills kicker Tyler Bass has handled every kickoff for the Buffalo Bills this year until Monday night against the Minnesota Vikings. This week, punter Tommy Doman handled those duties. He immediately showed why Buffalo might want to go with him moving forward. (I think I am kidding.)

On the second kickoff of the game, Doman met the Vikings returner near the 40 and dislodged the ball. The Vikings immediately caught the loose ball in the air, but Doman is credited with a forced fumble.

After the game, kicker Tyler Bass said the reason for the change was to "give another look". If Doman is going to hit like that, we should assume he's going to do it, right?

Doman's punts weren't great on Monday, which is a stark contract from the rest of the season. Multiple touchbacks led to better-than-expected field position for the Vikings. He had been very good to this point. We think he'll get it cleaned up going forward.

#2765. Davis puts on a show, Dybantsa flashes potential in loss to Pistons

The Washington Wizards got 44 points and 13 rebounds from Anthony Davis, and very little from anyone else, and lost to the Detroit Pistons, 122-111.

It was Washington's fourth straight loss as the team has struggled to generate effective offense or maintain stout defense.

Davis put on a show, especially in the first half, dominating the center-less Detroit lineup. He scored 30 points in the first half on 10-11 shooting from the floor. The Wizards headed to the locker room down 10 because the rest of the team shot 10-30.

AJ Dybantsa shows big time potential in Wizards loss to the Detroit Pistons. | Getty Images

For the game, Davis shot 16-21. The rest of the team: 25-68. Davis used 25 offensive possessions to generate 41 points. His teammates used 78 possessions to produce 70 points. As the great Fred Katz used to say, "Yikes guys."

The other major redeeming feature of the game was the play of No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybantsa, who had the most spectacular replacement level game I've ever seen. I can't decide which plays impressed me the most:

The lightning Euro-step drive in transition that froze John Collins and ended with a two-handed dunk

The drive that included getting fouled by Cade Cunningham out top, and ended with a cuffed dunk on Collins

The fake drive to attack a closeout that led to a relocation stepback three from the corner

That doesn't include his relentless defensive effort and the constant pressure he put on the Detroit defense. Or his duel with Cunningham that was massively entertaining.

Or when he battled Ron Holland for a loose ball, inadvertently slapped him in the face, and then spent a chunk of the break while refs watched the replay reviewing the play on the arena screen with Detroit's Daniss Jenkins.

The five turnovers and below average turnovers undermined his overall value for the game, but the highlights were big time plays, and the defensive impact was great from a 19-year-old rookie.

The Peacock broadcast format is great, and I hope it catches on around the league. Embedding the analysts on the benches is a genius innovation — especially when they share what the coaches are telling their players.

Bilal Coulibaly missed the game with a left hand injury that I'm pretty sure happened a couple games ago.

Will Riley entered the game in the first half, and almost immediately gave up one of the easiest drives in Cunningham's career. Zero resistance. Not even turnstile level defense.

Around 8:41 in the second quarter, Davis got an open three because Trae Young sprinted off screens, turned the corner and got into the paint. His effort on the play forced the help defender to commit (not coming over would have conceded a layup), which left Davis wide open at the three-point line. Young made the pass, and Davis converted.

When I looked at my notes, I discovered one more Dybantsa play that I'd forgotten — in the second quarter, he threw a fake so fast and convincing that Kevin Huerter stepped in the wrong direction. Dybantsa went past him for a layup.

Detroit opened the second half with Duncan Robinson getting a four-point play on what I thought was a bad call on Young. The Wizards started the period with a turnover, and then followed it up with an atrocious possession that ended with Dybantsa being forced to take a deep three with the shot clock running out. The team had tried — and failed — to feed Kyshawn George in the post against the diminutive Jenkins. They then ran multiple screens that finally got a switch that gave Dybantsa a mismatch…and not enough time to attack it.

Peaccock's Austin Rivers reported that during a third quarter timeout, Wizards coach Brian Keefe urged the team to improve their effort. His critique included Davis, who'd just given up a backcut dunk to Cunningham, which included an and-one free throw. "Let's not wait until the next game," Keefe said, according to Rivers. "Let's do it now."

George needs to figure out to play on offense without turning it over so much. He had five more turnovers last night. On one in the fourth quarter, he drove into the paint, couldn't get to the rim, and picked up his dribble. Stuck, and with the three-second count ticking, he attempted a ridiculous pass out with Ausar Thompson in the vicinity. The pass was stolen, of course.

I wrote this in the fourth quarter, but I could have written it in any period: The Wizards cannot figure out how to initiate their offense. Dybantsa set a screen for George. George came up to set a ball screen for Davis. But, Davis went nowhere. George drifted a little and the possession just stalled. Davis finally tossed up a three, which missed. The offensive design was fine, though perhaps not with Davis as the ball handler.

A few minutes later, the Wizards ran a similar set but with Davis screening for George. Davis rolled hard, George made a crisp pass, and Davis converted the layup.

Thompson had an amazing block on Alex Sarr with around four minutes left in the game. He met Sarr at the rim, contested with with verticality, went up higher despite being several inches smaller, and swatted the dunk attempt.

Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made).

eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot)

TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions)

FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts)

PPA is my overall production metric, which credits players for things they do that help a team win (scoring, rebounding, playmaking, defending) and dings them for things that hurt (missed shots, turnovers, bad defense, fouls).

PPA is a per possession metric designed for larger data sets. In small sample sizes, the numbers can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn't much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results.

POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game.

ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist.

USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median last season was 17.7%.

ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers.

+PTS = "Plus Points" is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0.

Players are sorted by total production in the game.

#2764. The Real Reason The Mets Should Target These 3 Pitchers Now

The New York Mets are expected to spend a record amount of money to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. This move would give the team a true ace to lead the starting rotation for the next several years. Even with Skubal on the roster, the Mets still lack depth and need another reliable starter to win in the playoffs. The front office should look to the trade market to find a partner for Skubal rather than relying only on free agency.

Acquiring a second starter through a trade allows the Mets to control costs and secure long-term value. The team has young players and prospects that other clubs want in exchange for established pitchers. Three specific names stand out as the best targets to pair with Skubal and build a dominant rotation for the upcoming season. These pitchers offer different contracts and levels of control that fit the needs of the New York team.

Logan Webb from the San Francisco Giants is the top target for the Mets to acquire via trade. According to Rising Apple, he placed within the top 11 of the NL Cy Young competition annually between 2022 and 2025. Webb is an ace who would serve as the number two starter behind Skubal and push Nolan McLean to the number three spot. He has a career average of 3.8 bWAR and has shown he can be worth 5.6 bWAR at his best. While the Giants declined to trade him mid-season, they may reconsider this winter if presented with the proper offer.

The financial terms of Webb's deal make him an attractive option for the Mets to consider. A five-year, $90 million extension signed with San Francisco leaves him with two additional years of team control. This contract leaves $47 million remaining on the deal, which Rising Apple notes could be a bargain for the Mets. Securing a pitcher with this level of production and cost control is rare in the current market. The team would gain a reliable innings eater who does not need to be re-signed soon.

Webb's presence would immediately stabilize the rotation alongside Skubal and give the Mets a clear advantage. He brings a track record of success against tough lineups in the National League. The Giants have a surplus of pitching talent that could allow them to move Webb if the Mets offer a strong package of prospects. This trade would solve the need for a number two starter without costing the team a massive free agent contract in the future.

Emerson Hancock of the Seattle Mariners is another excellent target because he comes with multiple years of team control. He has four years of control left and will not be a free agent until 2031 according to Rising Apple. The 27-year-old right-hander posted a 3.57 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 2.7 bWAR in 25 starts last season. He struck out 126 batters in 138.2 innings while maintaining a 109 ERA+ and a 4.00 FIP. These numbers show he is a solid mid-rotation starter who can grow into a bigger role.

With a surplus of young starting pitchers, the Seattle Mariners were receptive to moving Hancock before the trade deadline. They could revisit dealing him this offseason as they look to improve their offense which struggled last year. Since Jerry DiPoto prioritizes bats over pitchers, the Mets possess a glut of young middle infielders available for exchange. Sports Illustrated reports that Seattle has a full five-man rotation including Logan Gilbert, Bryan Woo and Bryce Miller. This depth allows them to trade a starter like Hancock without hurting their own rotation.

Trading for Hancock would give the Mets a pitcher with significant security for the next four seasons. He is young enough to develop further while providing immediate value in the rotation. The Mets could use one of their extra infield prospects to complete this deal and address a need for the Mariners. This move would add a cost-controlled arm that fits perfectly alongside Skubal and Webb if the team pursues all three.

Drew Rasmussen from the Tampa Bay Rays is a third option that the Mets should consider despite the risks involved. The Rays just exercised his $20 million club option for 2027 according to Rising Apple. This means he has only one year of control remaining before he hits free agency. The team would be taking a chance on a rental pitcher who might leave after the next season. This strategy mirrors what the Mets did with Freddy Peralta last year, a move that did not work out well for them.

Erik Neander, the Rays president of baseball operations, recently informed reporters that the club plans to retain Rasmussen as their rotation leader. This statement makes landing Rasmussen seem like a long shot for the Mets. Nevertheless, the Mets ought to contact the Rays to determine if they can extract him from those plans. He would provide a major boost to the rotation if he stays healthy and performs well for the duration of his contract. The risk is high but the reward of adding another quality starter is significant.

Possessing controllable starting pitching and infield depth, the Mets could persuade the Rays to alter their stance. A trade for Rasmussen would require the Mets to give up valuable assets that they might want to keep for the long term. The team must decide if the immediate need for a starter outweighs the risk of losing him after one year. If the Mets can negotiate a deal, they would add a proven arm to their rotation for the next season.

The trade market offers the Mets a better way to build their rotation than relying solely on free agency. David Stearns has restocked the farm system with strong deadline deals and has many attractive trade chips available. Yahoo Sports highlights that the Mets hold a surplus of young middle infielders capable of being traded for a substantial return. Teams looking to make deals often prefer trading for players with control rather than paying high free agent salaries.

The risk of losing a player after one year means the Mets must weigh the cost carefully. If they trade for Rasmussen, they need to ensure the return they get is worth the risk. Building a championship rotation requires a mix of aces and reliable mid-rotation starters. #2760. Wemby is an alien; Phoenix is painfully human

There were no illusions of grandeur entering the Suns' matchup against the San Antonio Spurs on Monday night. The game would serve as a litmus test, an opportunity to see where Phoenix stood against one of the best teams in the NBA, and it played out pretty much as you might have expected. The Spurs are one of those unique teams that have the advantage of youth on their side, and when you add the fact that they have an alien in Victor Wembanyama patrolling both ends of the floor, defeating them is going to be a difficult task for every team across the Association throughout the season.

Victor Wembanyama is a demigod, an unstoppable force who, at this point, is toying with the sport of basketball. His impact on both ends of the floor is unlike anything we've seen. He possesses the size of Shawn Bradley, whom many of us grew up watching, but his game extends far beyond simply being big. The way he defends, the way he deters anyone who ventures inside the three-point arc, and the constant threat of his mere existence manipulate the game in a manner that leaves you shrugging your shoulders and sighing.

As for the Suns? They did a good job taking care of the basketball, committing only seven turnovers. But they were outscored 62-48 in the paint, 20-10 in second-chance points, and 19-10 in fast-break points. They were also outrebounded by 20, with San Antonio holding a commanding 55-35 advantage on the glass.

The Suns have made progress over the past week, but there's still a considerable gap between where they are and where the Western Conference's elite reside. San Antonio exposed the same deficiencies we've been discussing all season, particularly Phoenix's inability to control the glass and protect the paint. There's no shame in losing to a team featuring a generational talent like Wembanyama. But the manner in which you lose can tell you plenty about how far you still have to go.

It's not often the guy who scores under 10 points gets the Bright Side Baller, but the community here knows ball. The impact Ryan Dunn had in the victory over the Rockets was stellar, as he was a disruptor in every sense of the word.
