#2637. Inter Milan U19: Team Analysis – MH

von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

Inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

Inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

To build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

The primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

If only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be quickly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

To effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

Through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

Even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

This three-man buildup creates new passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

Due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

Additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

The follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

One of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

While striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

The pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

Another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

Depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

Once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

Especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

As the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

Inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

In possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2636. Doc Rivers says 'difficult' Giannis Antetokounmpo 'didn't want to be the bad guy' while forcing Bucks exit

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Milwaukee Bucks coach Doc Rivers said Giannis Antetokounmpo was difficult to coach and "didn't want to be the bad guy" amid the saga that ultimately led to his trade to the Miami Heat this summer.

Rivers, who coached the Bucks for two and a half seasons from 2024-26, said on "The Bill Simmons Podcast" that the ordeal dragged on for so long because Antetokounmpo "kept yo-yoing" with his desire to leave Milwaukee. Antetokounmpo never publicly requested a trade.

Like any small-market star, Antetokounmpo had been the subject of trade rumors since he emerged as an MVP-caliber player, but the questions about his future really amped up in recent years as the Bucks' title window closed and he moved closer to unrestricted free agency.

The Bucks had the opportunity to trade Antetokounmpo after the 2024-25 season, which ended with another first-round exit after Damian Lillard tore his Achilles tendon. Instead, Milwaukee waived Lillard and stretched his contract, which will now be on their books until 2030, and signed Myles Turner to a four-year, $108 million deal in a desperate attempt to keep Antetokounmpo around. The plan did not work; the Bucks missed the playoffs last season for the first time since 2016, and eventually traded Antetokounmpo when it became clear that he would not sign an extension.

"In [Bucks general manager Jon Horst's] defense, I thought Giannis kept yo-yoing," Rivers said when discussing what went wrong in Milwaukee over the last few seasons. "When I look back on that whole situation, Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. He didn't want to be the bad guy. He wanted Jon and [co-owner Wes Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

Everyone could see that Antetokounmpo, who led the Bucks to the 2021 NBA championship, was torn about leaving the only franchise he had ever known, and the city where he had spent nearly half of his life, but it's still notable to hear Rivers confirm it.

Rivers' more interesting comments were about how hard it was for him to coach Antetokounmpo:

"He's not easy. He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy. I was telling someone this. He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have a super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing. And he really has only one way -- downhill, force, force, force. Every play, he wants to force it. I wish he'd learned how to execute better.

"He's one of those guys, you get a lot of them from the U.S., AAU guys that have never needed to execute, because they can do it on their own. But that doesn't help the team. I told Giannis this: The thing he still needs to learn is the value of execution. How important it is, when you're in practice and at shootaround, to lock in on execution. Now he has a coach who's as good as there is in execution."

Antetokounmpo is a unique player and, like many all-time greats, incredibly stubborn. Those qualities helped him grow into a two-time MVP and lead the Bucks to their first title in 50 years. They also made it challenging to build a roster around him and led him to play through injuries that should have kept him on the sideline.

There are certainly aspects of Antetokounmpo's style and approach that would make life difficult for any coach, but Rivers has been making excuses about his time with the Bucks since his introductory press conference, when he said, "I wouldn't wish this on anyone," about taking over a team with Antetokounmpo, Lillard and Khris Middleton mid-season.

It was also a bit strange to hear Rivers say that Antetokounmpo, who scored 50 points in a title-clinching game on 16 of 25 from the field and 17 of 19 from the free-throw line, needs to learn the value of execution.

Rivers was not retained after the 2026 season and Antetokounmpo, along with Bobby Portis, was traded to the Heat in June. In return, the Bucks received Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, three first-round picks, a second-round pick and a pick swap.

Both teams are off to rough starts this season. While the Bucks are 1-7 as they begin their rebuild, the Heat are 3-6. Antetokounmpo is averaging 27.3 points, 12.7 rebounds and 5.6 assists per game.

#2635. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni denies giving his fans the middle finger after division loss: 'Absolutely not'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia Eagles season isn't exactly going as planned, with a losing record and major injuries. When struggles come in sports, frustrations typically follow and Philly's head coach has been accused of letting out those frustrations with a well-known gesture after their 19-11 divisional loss to the New York Giants on Sunday, the team's first loss in Philadelphia to the Giants since 2013.

Nick Sirianni was called out for what some believe was the head coach giving fans the middle finger as he walked off the field after the Week 9 defeat. In the video, Sirianni looks at his hand, then the middle finger is raised higher than the others as he approaches the tunnel.

Nick Sirianni was asked if he was flipping fans off while walking off the field yesterday. "Absolutely not." #Eagles https://t.co/fqKylEJGxw

— Cory Nidoh (@Cory_Nidoh) November 9, 2026

Sirianni denies any ill will on whatever his hand was doing at the time, saying, "Absolutely not. That was a surprise to me. Absolutely not."

This is not the first time Sirianni and Eagles fans have clashed. In 2024, Sirianni was booed by some fans at Lincoln Financial Field, with some yelling for him to be fired during a game against the then 1-5 Cleveland Browns. Fans weren't happy that the Eagles were struggling, coming off a bye, against an easy opponent. Philadelphia went went on to win the game, though narrowly at 20-16.

As he was walking off the field, Sirianni cupped his ears and yelled at fans. At first, he said he was just "having fun" and was "excited to get the win," but then reversed his messaging, issuing an apology to Eagles fans.

"What I was really doing, I was trying to bring energy yesterday, energy, enthusiasm, and I'm sorry and disappointed on how my energy was directed at the end of the game," he said at the time. "And, you know, my energy should be all in on coaching, motivating and celebrating with our guys. And so I've got to have better wisdom and discernment of when to use that energy and that wasn't the time."

Another notable move from the head coach this Sunday was how long it took to start his press conference, with him taking the podium over an hour after the game ended. He said during that time he was talking to players and didn't reveal exactly what it was about. Typically, press conferences begin much sooner than that for a head coach, so many online pointed out the oddity.

The Eagles currently sit at 2-7 and are on a seven-game losing streak. This marks the worst start during Sirianni's time with the team. This marks the first time since 1999 that the team has started 2-7.

If Sirianni wasn't in the hot seat before (he was), he certainly is now after a bad divisional loss that put them in last in the NFC East.

#2634. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

#2631. Aleix García answers Andrich criticism with impressive performance in Leverkusen’s derby victory

The Spanish midfielder had come under scrutiny following Leverkusen’s 1-0 Europa League defeat to Marseille on Thursday, when Andrich publicly questioned his attitude after he failed to track back following a misplaced pass in the build-up to the winning goal.

However, García provided the perfect response in Köln, opening the scoring after just seven minutes with a stunning direct free-kick from around 20 metres. The 29-year-old went on to deliver an impressive all-round performance, earning Man of the Match recognition as Leverkusen secured an important three points.

Speaking after the game, teammate Ibrahim Maza praised García’s response to the difficult week, highlighting his mentality and importance to the team.

“That shows his attitude and mentality. Today you could see what an important player he is for us. He perhaps had a slightly difficult period in the last few games. That happens. He has played every game so far, and naturally that takes its toll physically and mentally,” Maza explained.

“Today he answered with an incredible goal, and afterwards he had the game under control. I thought it was a great reaction from him.”

Edmond Tapsoba also addressed the situation between García and Andrich, insisting that there were no lasting issues within the Leverkusen dressing room.

“We talk about it as a team. We don’t take it as a serious issue, we sort things out internally. We live like a family, and something like that can happen,” the defender explained.

Tapsoba added that the important thing was to take criticism in the right way and continue working together towards their collective ambitions.

Head coach Carles Martínez also played down the situation, explaining that the two midfielders have a good relationship and had spoken following the incident.

“The two have a good connection and talk to each other. Sometimes things are exaggerated on the outside. Inside, life goes on,” Martínez said.

The Leverkusen coach was also pleased with García’s response on the pitch, highlighting how the midfielder had approached the game with greater aggression.

“Errors are part of football. What matters is reacting and understanding why something happened. If the same situation comes around again, you have to deal with it differently. Today he was more aggressive,” Martínez added.

García’s contribution proved particularly important as Leverkusen ended a difficult run of results with a valuable derby victory. Patrik Schick doubled their advantage in the 85th minute before Said El Mala pulled one back for Köln in stoppage time.

The result leaves Leverkusen heading into the international break on a positive note, with García having delivered a timely reminder of his importance to the side.

#2627. Why NFL trade deadline evolved from afterthought to hectic: In-season transaction boom is league's new normal

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Less than a decade ago, it was common for the NFL to feature single-digit trades during the course of the regular season. The trade deadline was generally a snoozer in comparison to that of the other major American professional sports leagues, and the number of moves made at the buzzer could often be counted on one hand. That could not be further from the case anymore.

Twenty-four hours out from the 2026 trade deadline, there were 10 in-season trades in the books. That number will balloon in the final hours before the clock strikes 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 10. Star players could be on the move as Super Bowl contenders gear up for the stretch run and teams falling out of contention seek to jumpstart their rebuilds with premium draft capital. Basketball and baseball fans are used to seeing this flurry of transactions, but it is still relatively new to football fans. Just like in the other leagues, though, this boom is becoming the NFL's new normal.

Last year, there were 22 trades from the first day of the regular season through the deadline. That was the most in any year since at least 1995, according to NFL Research. A whopping 12 players and 14 picks were exchanged on deadline day alone. General managers were busier than ever. That was the extreme continuation of a trend that has been in effect since the mid-2010s, in which front offices mortgage their futures for instant-impact players or, conversely, sell off their most valuable assets to hoard draft picks.

Only once from 2010 through 2017 did the NFL log 12 or more in-season trades, according to the Spotrac trade tracker. Something flipped towards the end of the decade, because that number now represents the low-water mark since 2018.

Why the sudden uptick? There are fundamental processes in the NFL that make this league more trade-averse than other sports leagues, but changes to the calendar and new front-office philosophies have created pathways for teams to bypass some of the roadblocks.

Trading players in the NFL is not as simple as matching salaries. That is largely why player-for-player trades remain so rare. The way contracts are structured, with teams spreading bonuses out across multiple years, taking on dead money and being on the hook for some of the salary owed to the players they trade away, is sometimes prohibitive. Plus, the NFL has a hard salary cap, so unlike in the NBA, where teams use exceptions to go over the cap, or in MLB, where wealthy owners can pony up as much money as they please, all deals have to result in both teams remaining under that firm number.

Football is also not as plug-and-play as other sports. There are massive playbooks to learn, especially at the offensive skill positions. There is incredibly important timing to perfect, particularly for the quarterback-wide receiver tandem. With 11 players on the field at all times and complicated schemes to comprehend, anyone who joins a lineup in the middle of the season has a lot of learning to do on the fly.

The brevity of a 17-game regular season also keeps a larger percentage of the league in playoff contention deeper into the year compared to 82- or 162-game campaigns. The lack of non-contenders means fewer teams are willing to sell, and thus there is a smaller volume of available players.

Draft picks are also immensely valuable since teams have so many roster spots to fill. And at the same time, rosters are so large that fringe players around the 53-man cutoff can simply be released if the potential trade package is undesirable.

Until 2011, the NFL trade deadline was extremely early in the season. It landed on the Tuesday following Week 6, which was well before the midway point of the campaign. Teams were often still attempting to figure out where they stood in the pecking order when it came time to lock in their rosters. How could a general manager shop one of his stars on an expiring contract when they were not sure whether their team was in the mix for a postseason berth or not? They rarely did.

That changed in 2012 when the NFL and NFL Players Association agreed to move the deadline back by two weeks to the Tuesday following Week 8. And not long after the league adopted a 17th regular-season game, it moved the deadline back another week to where it stands now: The Tuesday after Week 9, which is effectively the midseason point.

It is far clearer where teams stand in the playoff picture after Week 9 than after Week 6. Look no further than the Indianapolis Colts, who emerged as one of the NFL's most aggressive sellers this year. Through six games, they were 2-4 and competitive enough in a couple of their losses to believe that they could right the ship. Now, after nine games, they are a measly 2-7 and own a five-game losing streak. Clearly out of the postseason hunt, they moved on from perennial Pro Bowlers in Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner.

Perhaps the single most impactful change in the rise of in-season trades comes from the mentality surrounding draft picks. While the value of Day 1 picks in the NFL is still tremendous, it is more common now than ever to see general managers move that sacred capital for players who can help them win at the highest level right away instead of a couple of years down the line. Nowhere is this clearer than in Los Angeles, where Rams general manager Les Snead birthed the "F them picks" mantra.

Each of those moves opened or extended the Rams' championship contention windows. They are bets on current stars and their ability to keep playing at a high level, compared to the risk of boom-or-bust picks in the late first round. In order to balance the roster, Snead relies on finding diamonds in the rough in the later rounds, which he has been highly successful at pulling off.

This model delivered a Super Bowl and proved to other teams that it is a viable strategy for roster construction. In the copycat league that is the NFL, the Rams are no longer the only team to go all in to fuel championship runs.

Snead even has direct disciples putting his methodology to practice in other places. Jacksonville Jaguars general manager James Gladstone worked under Snead's tutelage in various roles for nine years before he landed a GM job of his own. On Monday, he pulled off two trades in which he swapped draft picks for immediate-impact players. They may not have been Day 1 picks, but they were draft capital nonetheless.

Draft picks are still gold, even in this era where they are moved like never before. General managers who want the best of both worlds -- to hoard picks and secure immediate impacts -- can balance the two, but they have to be creative. Enter the pick swap. Instead of one team netting a draft pick while the other loses one, pick swaps allow teams to generate value in the aggregate while retaining at least some capital. If a player is valued around a late-Day 2 pick, the buying team could send a second-rounder and receive a Day 3 pick in return along with that player.

Compensatory picks also give general managers the flexibility to take swings at available players. If there is a veteran on an expiring contract who can join a team as a half-season rental, the buying franchise may give up a third-round pick or worse to acquire them, knowing that they can recoup the pick if the player leaves in free agency.

Gladstone himself pulled off a masterful move ahead of Tuesday's deadline by factoring compensatory picks into the equation. He reached a deal with the New Orleans Saints that sent Davon Godchaux to Jacksonville in exchange for a conditional 2028 sixth-round pick. That pick would become a 2027 sixth-rounder if the Jaguars acquire one through another trade or through the compensatory formula. In essence, Gladstone traded a pick he does not even own yet.

So many things in football are cyclical, but the surge in trade deadline action has staying power. Changes at the league level with regard to scheduling have made it more viable, and general managers are as aggressive as ever in a "what have you done for me lately" world. Now that front offices have another tool at their disposal in roster construction, it will only become more mainstream. The cat is out of the bag, and it will be hard to put it back in.

#2626. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2625. Warriors' Kristaps Porziņģis stepping away from basketball to deal with ongoing health issues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis announced Friday that he has "made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love" as he continues to deal with mysterious health issues. It's unclear when, or if, the 31-year-old Porziņģis will return to the court.

Porziņģis has not played for the Warriors this season and reports earlier this week indicated that the team is withholding payments from him. He signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer, but the second year of the deal only has a $3 million guarantee.

Here is Porziņģis' full statement announcing his decision to step away from basketball:

This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated.

I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love.

In this situation, I want to show the utmost respect for the Golden State Warriors and work with them to find a solution that makes sense.

I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support.

Porziņģis' career has been defined by health problems. He's played more than 57 games just three times since he was drafted No. 4 overall by the New York Knicks in 2015, and has dealt with significant injuries, including a torn ACL that cost him the entire 2018-19 season. In recent years, he's been limited by this mysterious illness that first became an issue in Boston during the 2024-25 season.

Porziņģis started dealing with extreme fatigue and previously disclosed a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, which is characterized by rapid changes in heart rate when a person stands up and can lead to exhaustion and dizziness.

"You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that," Porziņģis said ahead of last season. "At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."

Over the last three seasons with the Celtics, Atlanta Hawks and Warriors, Porziņģis has only played 74 games. He has been away from the Warriors since late September and released a previous statement in mid-October shutting down rumors that he had been diagnosed with HIV or AIDS. At that point, the Warriors said Porziņģis would be out indefinitely.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

The Warriors hoped that Porziņģis would play a big role this season as a floor-spacing big, especially while Jimmy Butler (torn ACL) and Moses Moody (torn patellar tendon) remain sidelined. Instead, it seems more likely that he will never play for the franchise again.

The Warriors have reportedly been trying to trade Porziņģis to use his $20 million cap figure, as explained by CBS Sports' Sam Quinn:

While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Despite Porziņģis' absence, the Warriors are off to a 6-3 start, putting them in seventh place in the extremely crowded Western Conference standings. Rookie big man Yaxel Lendeborg has stepped up in Porziņģis' place and provided a major boost on both ends of the floor.

Through nine games, Lendeborg is averaging 21 points, 7.1 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 1.1 steals while shooting 49.2% from the field, including 39.6% from 3-point range.

#2623. MLB rumors: Why the Dodgers could be Tarik Skubal or bust; Red Sox looking for pitching depth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.
